meta.blurb: In 1930 Gandhi walked nearly four hundred kilometres to the sea to pick up a handful of salt, and mass protest followed. Why? Follow salt from desert caravans and Roman roads to hated taxes, and see how it shaped wars and freedom.
meta.bible: Salt: sodium chloride; the body needs some. Brine: salty water. Rock Salt: buried beds from ancient seas. Natron: salty mineral used by the ancient Egyptians. Garum: Roman fermented fish sauce. Amole: Ethiopian salt bars used as money. Gabelle: the French salt tax, abolished 1790. Sichuan: region of China with very deep brine wells. Han: Chinese dynasty that ran a salt monopoly. Hallstatt: salt mine in the Austrian Alps worked for more than three thousand years. Salzburg: Austrian city named for salt. Droitwich, Nantwich, Northwich, Middlewich: English salt towns; Cheshire. Via Salaria: the Salt Road of ancient Rome; Ostia; Tiber; Rome. Ibn Battuta: Moroccan traveller who saw Taghaza in 1352. Taghaza: Saharan salt town. Timbuktu, Mali, Sahel, Sahara: places of the gold and salt trade. Danakil Depression, Ethiopia, Afar: people who cut salt today. Maras: salt pools in Peru. Maya, Mexico, Peru, Andes. Luneburg, Lubeck: German towns on the Old Salt Road. Hanseatic League: trading alliance of northern towns. Venice: republic made rich partly by salt. Wieliczka, Krakow, Poland: salt mine of the thirteenth century. Basques, Newfoundland, Atlantic: salted cod. France, Napoleon, French Revolution. Moscow, Russia, tsar, Salt Riot of 1648. Turks Islands, Caribbean: enslaved salt rakers. American Revolution, Civil War, Union, Confederacy, Saltville, Virginia. Erie Canal opened 1825; Syracuse, Onondaga Lake, Onondaga, New York, Salt City, Great Lakes, Hudson River. Leblanc and Solvay: industrial processes for making soda ash. Switzerland, United States, Iodine: added to salt from the 1920s. Goitre: swelling of the neck. British, Britain, India: the salt tax. Mohandas Gandhi: led the Salt March from 12 March 1930, about 240 miles or nearly four hundred kilometres, ending at Dandi on 6 April 1930; Ahmedabad; India free in 1947. Sumo, Japan, Hebrew Bible, Covenant. Salar de Uyuni: salt flat in Bolivia; Lithium; Chile, Argentina, Bolivia, Canada, China, Germany. Europe, Africa, Asia, Italy, Spain, Mediterranean, Baltic Sea, North Sea, Earth, Lent, Church, Catholics, Roman. Added for the full-length book: Wadi Natrun, Egypt: natron lakes; mummies dried in natron for about forty days. Mesopotamia, Tigris, Euphrates: irrigation brought salt to the fields. Dead Sea: far saltier than the ocean; Hebrew name means the Salt Sea. Phoenicians, Tyre, Sidon: sea traders. Homer: called salt divine. Pompeii, Vesuvius: garum town, buried in the year 79. Livy, Cato, Pliny: Roman writers; Marcus Livius, nicknamed Salinator, taxed salt in 204 BCE. Guérande: French salt marsh. Sichuan wells: bamboo cable and iron bit; a well of 1835 about a thousand metres deep; natural gas piped through bamboo; Han monopoly; Discourses on Salt and Iron, 81 BCE; Yangzhou: city of rich salt merchants. Taoudenni: Saharan salt mine that replaced Taghaza; Sahel. Maya, Belize, Aztec, Texcoco, Tenochtitlan, Huixtocihuatl: goddess of salt; Maras, Inca; Tibet: yak caravans; Japan, Shinto, Sumo; Namak halal: Urdu and Hindi phrase, true to the salt. Lüneburg, Lübeck: Old Salt Road, about a hundred kilometres; Scania: herring fisheries; Bay of Bourgneuf: bay salt; Beukelszoon: legendary Dutch herring gutter; Chioggia, Ferrara: Venice and the war of the 1480s. Wieliczka, Bochnia, Krakow: Polish salt mines; Saint Kinga's chapel; Salzach, Hallein, Wolf Dietrich: the Salt War of 1611; Cheshire, Domesday Book 1086; rock salt found near Northwich in 1670; River Weaver. Brittany: free of the gabelle; the gabelle began in the 1300s, Napoleon's salt tax 1806 to 1945. Alexis: tsar; Morozov: minister whose salt tax of 1646 was withdrawn in 1647; the Salt Riot of 1648. Columbus, Magellan, James Lind: scurvy, 1747; Basque fishermen; Newfoundland, Grand Banks: cod; Lent; West India cod; Bermudians, Salt Cay, Turks Islands: slavery abolished in the British Empire in 1834. American Revolution salt shortage; Onondaga: salt springs; Simon Le Moyne, 1654; Erie Canal, 1825, about 360 miles; Cincinnati: Porkopolis; Saltville, Virginia: attacked October and December 1864; Avery Island, Louisiana. Leblanc: process of 1791, died poor in 1806; Alkali Act, 1863; Solvay: ammonia process from the 1860s; Brunner and Mond: Northwich, 1870s; Liverpool, St Helens, Widnes. East India Company, Bengal: salt monopoly; the Great Hedge of India, more than two thousand miles, given up about 1879. Gandhi: letter to Lord Irwin on 2 March 1930; Sabarmati ashram; seventy-eight walkers; twenty-four days; Gujarat; Gandhi was sixty; Sarojini Naidu: led the Dharasana raid on 21 May 1930; Webb Miller: American reporter; Yerwada: prison; Gandhi-Irwin Pact, March 1931. Appert: canning, 1809; Dunedin: frozen meat ship, 1882; David Marine: Akron, Ohio, goitre trial 1917 to 1922; iodised salt in Switzerland 1922 and the United States 1924. Salar de Uyuni: lithium brine. Other names used: Bavaria, Carpathian, Haudenosaunee, Gujarat, Surat, Arabian Sea, Karadi, Stoneman, Angus Smith, Warren Hastings, Indian National Congress, Pyrenees, Biscay, Dharasana. Voice and tone: curious, clear and warm; the facts are real and hedged where scholars disagree; no invented quotes or numbers; hard labour and smuggling are told plainly, without gore.

beats.scene: A hand shakes salt from a glass shaker onto a plate of food
beats.summary: Introduction: salt is tiny and ordinary, yet it has shaped history.

beats.scene: Close view of white cubic salt crystals on a dark spoon
beats.summary: Salt is sodium and chlorine joined together, and its crystals are tiny cubes.

beats.scene: A cyclist pauses to drink water beside a quiet country road
beats.summary: The body uses salt to carry signals along nerves and to make muscles work.

beats.scene: A farm worker wipes sweat from his face under a hot sun
beats.summary: People lose salt in sweat, and it must be replaced from food.

beats.scene: A mother wipes a child's tear while both sit near the sea
beats.summary: Blood and tears taste salty, and the body keeps its salt level steady.

beats.scene: A bowl of plain boiled rice and a glass of water on a table
beats.summary: The body cannot make salt, so people have always had to find it.

beats.scene: A tired traveller sits in the shade, holding his head and a water bottle
beats.summary: Too little salt can cause weakness, cramps and confusion, and it can make people ill.

beats.scene: A cow licks a white block of salt in a green pasture
beats.summary: Animals and people crave salt, and the tongue is built to notice it.

beats.scene: A measuring spoon holds a small heap of salt beside a loaf of bread
beats.summary: A body needs only a little salt each day, much less than many people now eat.

beats.scene: A traveller with a pack crosses a map marked with deserts, seas and mountains
beats.summary: The book will follow salt across the world and through time.

beats.scene: White salt crystals glitter along the edge of a shallow sea
beats.summary: Seawater holds about three and a half parts of salts in a hundred, mostly ordinary salt.

beats.scene: Pale crusts of salt ring the edge of a still lake in dry hills
beats.summary: Salt lakes in dry lands have no outlet, so water leaves only by evaporation and the salt stays.

beats.scene: Steam rises from a spring beside a hillside of pale stone
beats.summary: Brine springs rise where underground water has passed through buried beds of salt.

beats.scene: A cutaway of the earth shows thick white layers below layers of clay
beats.summary: Rock salt is what remains of ancient seas that dried up millions of years ago.

beats.scene: A tall mound of earth rises from a plain, with salt layers cut away
beats.summary: Buried salt is light and can slowly push upward through the rock above it, forming salt domes.

beats.scene: Deer and wild cattle lick a white patch of earth at a forest edge
beats.summary: Wild animals travel far to reach salt licks, where salty earth or spring water appears at the surface.

beats.scene: Hunters in animal skins follow a narrow trail toward a clearing with salty earth
beats.summary: Early hunters probably followed animals to the licks and so found the first salt.

beats.scene: A hunter roasts meat over a fire beside a stream
beats.summary: Hunters who ate much meat and blood probably got enough salt without adding any.

beats.scene: Farmers harvest golden grain in a field beside a village
beats.summary: When people began farming, their meals of grain and vegetables held little salt, so they began to add it.

beats.scene: Villagers boil spring water in clay pots beside a stream in ancient Romania
beats.summary: In Romania, people boiled spring brine in clay pots some eight thousand years ago, among the earliest known salt works.

beats.scene: Fish hang on drying racks beside a barrel packed with salt
beats.summary: Salt keeps food by drawing out water, so the germs that spoil it cannot grow.

beats.scene: Fishermen split and salt their catch on a stony beach beside their boats
beats.summary: Fish was split, salted and dried, which let coastal peoples trade their catch far inland.

beats.scene: A butcher hangs a pig's leg above a wooden tub full of coarse salt
beats.summary: Meat was cured with salt as ham, bacon and salt pork, which kept for a long time.

beats.scene: Olives and white cheese float in jars of brine on a market table
beats.summary: Olives and some cheeses are kept in brine, a strong solution of salt in water.

beats.scene: A cook packs shredded cabbage and salt tightly into a large crock
beats.summary: Salt lets friendly bacteria ferment cabbage and other vegetables into sauerkraut and kimchi.

beats.scene: A cook stirs a pot of fermenting beans beside barrels of soy sauce
beats.summary: Salt makes soy sauce and miso possible, by fermenting beans and grain for months.

beats.scene: A baker salts a bowl of dough beside a plain unsalted loaf
beats.summary: Salt also improves taste, which is why cooks use it in bread, cheese and almost every kind of dish.

beats.scene: Pigs are led across a snowy farmyard as barrels stand ready by the door
beats.summary: Farm families slaughtered animals in autumn and salted the meat to last through winter.

beats.scene: Travellers and soldiers set out on a long road with sacks of dried food
beats.summary: Salted food let armies, travellers and ships carry their meals for months at a time.

beats.scene: A king's steward unlocks a heavy storehouse door above a pile of salt sacks
beats.summary: Whoever controlled salt controlled the food supply, which gave salt a power no spice or jewel could match.

beats.scene: Workers rake shallow ponds of seawater drying in the sun beside the sea
beats.summary: In sunny places, seawater was let into shallow pans and left to evaporate, leaving salt behind.

beats.scene: A worker in a straw hat drags a wooden rake across a grey marsh
beats.summary: In places like Guérande in France, salt workers still rake the crystals by hand from clay ponds.

beats.scene: A woman stirs a large pot of brine over a fire
beats.summary: In cold, wet places, people boiled brine in pots and pans over fires, using enormous amounts of fuel.

beats.scene: Woodcutters haul logs from a thinned forest toward smoking furnaces
beats.summary: Boiling salt used so much fuel that the cost of wood was often greater than the cost of the work.

beats.scene: Miners with picks cut a wide hall in rock salt, leaving thick pillars
beats.summary: Rock salt was mined by cutting out rooms and leaving pillars of salt to hold up the roof.

beats.scene: Miners with torches carry salt blocks out of a dark tunnel in the Alps
beats.summary: The Hallstatt salt mines in Austria were worked for thousands of years and made the region rich.

beats.scene: Archaeologists brush a scrap of old cloth from a salty wall inside a mine
beats.summary: Salt preserved cloth, leather, tools and food scraps in the Hallstatt mine, so archaeologists can see ancient life.

beats.scene: A rich grave holds a bronze sword, glass beads and amber beside a chief
beats.summary: Graves near Hallstatt held costly goods from far away, which suggests the salt trade brought wealth.

beats.scene: Water pumps into the ground through a pipe while brine flows from another
beats.summary: In modern salt works, water is pumped down into a salt bed and the brine is drawn back up.

beats.scene: A tall silver vessel stands at a modern salt works beside pipes and gauges
beats.summary: Modern vacuum pans boil brine at low pressure, so far less fuel is needed than for an open pan over a fire.

beats.scene: Workers drive a long bamboo cable into the ground beside a tall wooden frame
beats.summary: In Sichuan, China, drillers sank very deep brine wells using bamboo cables and iron bits.

beats.scene: Men jump on a wooden lever as an iron bit pounds rock
beats.summary: Drillers lifted and dropped a heavy iron bit on a bamboo cable, slowly breaking the rock below.

beats.scene: A tall wooden derrick stands above a narrow shaft lined with bamboo
beats.summary: Over the centuries Sichuan wells grew deeper, and one dug in 1835 reached about a thousand metres.

beats.scene: Water buffalo turn a huge wooden drum to raise a bamboo tube
beats.summary: Animals turned great drums to haul up the brine in long bamboo tubes.

beats.scene: A bamboo pipe carries a gas flame to a row of boiling iron pans
beats.summary: Drillers sometimes struck natural gas, and the people of Sichuan piped it through bamboo to boil brine.

beats.scene: A scribe records numbers while iron bars and salt sacks are stacked behind him
beats.summary: Under the Han dynasty about two thousand years ago, the state took control of salt and iron production.

beats.scene: Scholars in long robes argue with officials around a low table
beats.summary: In 81 BCE officials and scholars debated the monopoly in a famous discussion recorded as the Discourses on Salt and Iron.

beats.scene: A tax officer stands by a salt market with a ledger and scales
beats.summary: Rulers everywhere taxed salt because everyone needed it, few people made it, and it was easy to count.

beats.scene: Soldiers march along a new road past labourers building a long wall
beats.summary: Salt money paid for armies, roads and canals, and at times it made up a large share of imperial revenue.

beats.scene: A rich merchant's house with a garden pond stands beside a canal
beats.summary: Merchants who held salt licences grew very rich, and some, as in the city of Yangzhou, built grand gardens.

beats.scene: Workers collect pale mineral crusts beside a dry lake in Egypt
beats.summary: Egyptians gathered natron, a salty mineral, from dry lakes such as those of Wadi Natrun.

beats.scene: Priests in jackal masks lay a wrapped body on a stone table
beats.summary: Egyptians buried the dead by drying the body in natron for about forty days before wrapping it.

beats.scene: A scribe compares a drying fish and a drying body on two wooden tables
beats.summary: Mummies lasted because dryness stops decay, the same principle that keeps salted fish and meat.

beats.scene: Fishermen on the Nile haul nets full of fish toward drying racks
beats.summary: Egyptians also dried and salted fish and waterbirds, which fed the cities of the Nile.

beats.scene: A potter and a washerwoman use white powder beside a furnace and a basin
beats.summary: Natron was also used for cleaning and for making glass, so it was valuable well beyond the tomb.

beats.scene: Farmers stand in a flat field dusted white with salt beside an irrigation canal
beats.summary: In Mesopotamia, irrigation brought salt to the surface, and some scholars think this hurt the farmers' wheat.

beats.scene: A floating swimmer reads a scroll in the glittering Dead Sea
beats.summary: The Dead Sea is far saltier than the ocean, so no fish can live in it, and the Hebrew name means the Salt Sea.

beats.scene: A trading ship with a striped sail leaves a harbour loaded with clay jars
beats.summary: Phoenician traders probably carried salted fish and salt across the Mediterranean.

beats.scene: A Greek market stall displays salted fish from the Black Sea
beats.summary: Greek cities imported salted fish, and Athens bought large amounts from the Black Sea region.

beats.scene: A priest sprinkles salt on a sacrificial animal beside an altar
beats.summary: The Greek poet Homer called salt divine, and Greeks used it in their religious offerings.

beats.scene: A paved road leads through marshes toward salt pans near the sea beside Rome
beats.summary: The Romans had salt pans near Ostia at the mouth of the Tiber, and tradition says the port was founded to guard them.

beats.scene: A line of carts and mules follows an old road through rolling hills
beats.summary: The Via Salaria, the Salt Road, was an old track along which salt travelled from the coast to the hills.

beats.scene: A Roman magistrate in a white toga fixes a price tablet above salt sacks
beats.summary: The Roman state took control of salt supplies, and in 204 BCE a censor named Livius taxed salt and was nicknamed Salinator.

beats.scene: A Roman soldier receives a small leather bag from an officer
beats.summary: The English word salary comes from the Latin salarium, which may have meant money given to soldiers for salt, though scholars disagree.

beats.scene: A teacher writes Latin words on a slate beside a bowl of salad
beats.summary: Many English words come from the Latin sal: salad, sauce, sausage, and salami all began as salted things.

beats.scene: Workers pack fish in salt in a long stone factory beside a Spanish harbour
beats.summary: Salting fish was a large industry around the coasts of the empire, especially in Spain and North Africa.

beats.scene: Fish and salt are layered in a stone vat under a hot sun
beats.summary: Garum was a strong sauce made by letting fish and salt ferment in the sun for weeks.

beats.scene: Jars labelled with a maker's name stand in a ruined shop in Pompeii
beats.summary: Pompeii was famous for its garum, and jars marked with the names of makers have been found there.

beats.scene: An old farmer rubs salt into a hanging ham in a farmhouse kitchen
beats.summary: The Roman writer Cato described how farmers should salt hams, showing that preserving meat was a normal farm task.

beats.scene: Workers boil brine in lead pans at a Roman salt works
beats.summary: The Romans made salt in Britain, as at Droitwich, and salt roads there are still called salt ways.

beats.scene: A map shows desert in the north, savanna in the middle, forest south
beats.summary: West Africa had gold in the south and salt in the Sahara, and each region wanted what the other had.

beats.scene: A long line of camels carrying slabs of salt crosses golden desert dunes
beats.summary: Camel caravans carried salt south across the Sahara and brought gold and ivory north.

beats.scene: Houses built of white salt slabs stand in a hot desert settlement
beats.summary: Ibn Battuta saw Taghaza, a desert town built of salt, in 1352.

beats.scene: Workers in rough cloth dig salt from shallow pits in a bleak desert
beats.summary: Ibn Battuta found Taghaza harsh: bad water, flies, and workers who lived by digging salt.

beats.scene: A caravan leader checks ropes on two large salt slabs hanging on a camel
beats.summary: Salt was cut in big slabs, and each camel carried two on its sides across the desert.

beats.scene: Camels and men walk in a long line toward a distant red mountain
beats.summary: When Taghaza declined, the mines at Taoudenni took over, and the salt caravans still cross the desert today.

beats.scene: A busy market square in a mud-brick city with merchants, camels and scholars
beats.summary: Timbuktu grew rich as the meeting place of the salt and gold trade, and became a centre of learning.

beats.scene: A merchant balances a gold dust scale against a slab of salt
beats.summary: A story says salt was once sold for its weight in gold, which historians doubt, but both goods were certainly valuable.

beats.scene: A traveller buys cloth and spices with a flat bar of salt
beats.summary: In Ethiopia, bars of salt called amole served as small money until the twentieth century.

beats.scene: Workers cut salt blocks in a hot, flat desert in Ethiopia as camels wait
beats.summary: In the Danakil Depression of Ethiopia, Afar workers still cut salt by hand and send it out by camel.

beats.scene: Maya workers boil brine in clay pots over fires on a tropical coast
beats.summary: The Maya made salt on the coasts of Mexico and Belize by boiling brine in pots, and traded it inland.

beats.scene: A market in an island city with canals, salt cakes and a goddess statue
beats.summary: The Aztecs gathered salt from the lakes around Mexico and sold it in great markets, and honoured a goddess of salt.

beats.scene: Women gather salt from small terraced pools on a mountainside in Peru
beats.summary: At Maras in Peru, families still gather salt from hundreds of terraced pools fed by a salty spring.

beats.scene: A hunter and a trader exchange furs and salt beside a river
beats.summary: Peoples of North America gathered salt at springs and licks, and traded it over long distances.

beats.scene: A herder leads yaks loaded with white bags across a high stony plateau
beats.summary: On the Tibetan plateau, herders carry salt from salt lakes by yak and trade it for grain; butter tea also contains salt.

beats.scene: Workers pour sea water on a sandy beach and gather the salty sand
beats.summary: Japan had little rock salt, so people made salt by concentrating seawater on sand and then boiling it.

beats.scene: A host offers bread and a small dish of salt to a guest
beats.summary: In many countries a guest is welcomed with bread and salt, as a sign of friendship and respect.

beats.scene: Two men share a meal at a low table with a dish of salt
beats.summary: Having shared salt creates a bond of loyalty in many cultures, as in the Urdu and Hindi phrase namak halal.

beats.scene: A scroll and a lamp rest beside a small dish of salt on stone
beats.summary: The Hebrew Bible speaks of a covenant of salt, meaning a lasting promise, and the Gospel of Matthew calls believers the salt of the earth.

beats.scene: A wrestler throws a handful of salt into a ring before a match
beats.summary: In Japan, salt is a symbol of purity: sumo wrestlers throw it into the ring, and small piles are set at doors.

beats.scene: Brine bubbles in a row of lead pans inside a smoky German salt house
beats.summary: Lüneburg in Germany had salt springs worked for over a thousand years, and its salt works made the town rich.

beats.scene: A heavy cart and mules stand before a stack of logs
beats.summary: Lüneburg's works burned huge amounts of wood, and its pans used a great deal of fuel from the surrounding forests.

beats.scene: Carts of salt barrels roll along a muddy track through a dark forest
beats.summary: The Old Salt Road ran from Lüneburg to Lübeck on the Baltic, a journey of about a hundred kilometres.

beats.scene: Fishing boats crowd a cold Baltic coast as nets spill silver herring
beats.summary: Lübeck's merchants used the salt to preserve huge catches of herring from the rich fisheries of southern Sweden.

beats.scene: Workers gut herring on a quayside and pack them in barrels layered with salt
beats.summary: Herring were gutted at once and packed in layers of salt in barrels, then shipped to distant cities and monasteries.

beats.scene: Merchants in dark coats meet around a long table beneath ship models
beats.summary: The Hanseatic League was an alliance of northern trading towns, led by Lübeck, which grew rich on salt, herring and grain.

beats.scene: Sailing ships load white sacks at a sunny Atlantic salt marsh in France
beats.summary: Cheap sea salt from the Bay of Bourgneuf in France, called bay salt, reached the north in Dutch ships.

beats.scene: Dutch fishermen gut herring aboard a wide ship in rough North Sea water
beats.summary: Dutch fishermen gutted and salted herring at sea, and a legend says a man named Beukelszoon invented the method.

beats.scene: Boats loaded with salt sail toward a canal city of bell towers
beats.summary: Venice grew rich by making, importing and selling salt, and salt taxes paid much of the republic's costs.

beats.scene: A tall galley armed with cannons guards a salt convoy in the lagoon
beats.summary: Venice guarded its salt trade closely, had a special salt office, and fought wars partly to protect it.

beats.scene: Miners carve a chapel from walls of grey salt deep underground
beats.summary: The Wieliczka mine in Poland, worked from the thirteenth century, grew into a huge underground world.

beats.scene: A Polish king's treasurer counts coins beside a heavy chest of salt money
beats.summary: Salt from Wieliczka and Bochnia brought the Polish crown a large share of its income.

beats.scene: Horses are lowered by rope into a deep mine shaft as miners watch
beats.summary: Wieliczka was about three hundred metres deep, and horses worked underground in its tunnels for many years.

beats.scene: A chapel with salt chandeliers, carved statues and an altar glitters in lamplight
beats.summary: Miners carved chapels, altars and statues from the salt, including the great Chapel of Saint Kinga.

beats.scene: A princess drops a ring into a mine shaft in a green valley
beats.summary: A legend says that Princess Kinga's ring, thrown into a mine in Hungary, was found in Wieliczka's salt.

beats.scene: Flat wooden salt barges are poled down a swift river past a hilltop castle
beats.summary: The Austrian city of Salzburg is named for the salt barges on the river Salzach, and salt made its rulers rich.

beats.scene: Soldiers on horseback enter a walled city while townspeople watch from windows
beats.summary: In 1611 Bavaria invaded Salzburg in a quarrel over the salt trade, and the archbishop lost his throne.

beats.scene: A monk with a quill records salt houses in a large book
beats.summary: In England the Domesday Book of 1086 lists salt houses in the Cheshire towns Nantwich, Northwich and Middlewich.

beats.scene: Brine is boiled in huge iron pans inside a smoky building
beats.summary: For centuries the Cheshire wich houses boiled brine in pans, and the salt went by packhorse and cart.

beats.scene: Miners drive a shaft into a field near a river as boats wait
beats.summary: In 1670 a deep bed of rock salt was found near Northwich, and the river Weaver was later made navigable to carry the salt.

beats.scene: A king's officer reads a royal order aloud in a village square
beats.summary: In the 1300s the kings of France began taxing salt, and the tax, called the gabelle, lasted for centuries.

beats.scene: A map of France divided into patches of different colours with tax figures
beats.summary: The gabelle was unequal: some regions paid high rates, some paid low rates and a few were free.

beats.scene: A family looks at a heavy sack of salt left on their table
beats.summary: In the high-tax regions, households had to buy a fixed amount of salt every year, whether they needed it or not.

beats.scene: Guards in dark coats search a farmer's cart at a village gate at dusk
beats.summary: The tax was collected by agents called tax farmers, and their guards searched homes and carts for illegal salt.

beats.scene: A smuggler creeps along a dark hedge at night with a sack
beats.summary: Salt smugglers bought cheap salt in free regions and sold it in high-tax regions, creeping past guards at night.

beats.scene: A prisoner in chains is led toward a large rowing ship at a harbour
beats.summary: Smugglers risked heavy fines, prison, or being sent to the galleys, the oarsmen's benches of the king's warships.

beats.scene: A crowd in a village square burns tax papers while a drummer plays
beats.summary: In the French Revolution, citizens' complaints against the gabelle were loud, and it was abolished in 1790.

beats.scene: Napoleon in a bicorne hat signs a paper while clerks stack salt ledgers
beats.summary: Napoleon, wanting money for his wars, brought back a salt tax in 1806, and it lasted until 1945.

beats.scene: A Russian official in a fur hat reads a decree beside barrels of fish
beats.summary: In 1646 the Russian government taxed salt heavily, the price rose sharply and fish rotted for lack of salt, so the tax was withdrawn in 1647.

beats.scene: An angry crowd marches through a snowy street in old Moscow
beats.summary: In 1648 an angry crowd in Moscow rose up in the Salt Riot, and the tsar sent Morozov away.

beats.scene: Sailors lift heavy barrels of salted meat into a wooden ship
beats.summary: Salted beef and pork fed sailors on long voyages and made exploration possible.

beats.scene: A cook in a dark galley tries to cut a piece of hard meat
beats.summary: Sailors called salt beef salt horse, and soaked it before eating because it was so hard and salty.

beats.scene: Three small ships with square sails cross a wide grey ocean at sunrise
beats.summary: Explorers such as Columbus and Magellan sailed with salted meat and fish among their supplies.

beats.scene: A sailor with swollen gums sits on a bunk while another holds an orange
beats.summary: A diet of salted food and biscuit lacked fresh fruit, and many sailors fell ill with scurvy before a cure was understood.

beats.scene: Fishing boats of a Basque port sail out into a grey Atlantic dawn
beats.summary: Basque fishermen sailed far out into the Atlantic for cod, and some historians think they reached Newfoundland before Columbus, though this is disputed.

beats.scene: Fishermen work on a Newfoundland beach as cod dry on wooden racks
beats.summary: Cod was either salted heavily aboard the ship or split and dried on shore, and in both cases salt did the preserving.

beats.scene: A Portuguese cook soaks a stiff grey slab of dried fish in a basin
beats.summary: Salt cod suited the Catholic fast days when meat was forbidden, and Spain and Portugal still love their dried cod.

beats.scene: A ship's hold full of barrels and stiff dried fish bound for tropical islands
beats.summary: The cheapest grade of salt cod was shipped to the Caribbean to feed enslaved workers on sugar plantations.

beats.scene: Boats pull up to a flat white island where workers rake shallow ponds
beats.summary: Bermudian sailors raked salt from natural ponds on the Turks Islands in the Caribbean and shipped it to North America.

beats.scene: Workers rake salt into heaps on a bright island as a guard watches
beats.summary: The Turks Islands salt works depended on enslaved workers, who worked in heat and glare, until slavery ended in 1834.

beats.scene: A British warship blocks a harbour while townspeople watch empty salt warehouses
beats.summary: In the American Revolution, British blockades cut off imported salt, and the American army struggled to keep meat from spoiling.

beats.scene: People at the American coast boil seawater in iron kettles over many fires
beats.summary: Americans responded by boiling seawater in kettles along the coast, and state governments offered rewards for new salt works.

beats.scene: Native families scoop salt from a spring beside a lake as a priest watches
beats.summary: The Onondaga people of New York used the salt springs at Onondaga Lake long before settlers, and a French priest wrote about them in 1654.

beats.scene: Settlers boil brine in rows of iron kettles near a lake
beats.summary: After the Revolution, settlers boiled the Onondaga brine and sold the salt; New York State controlled the springs and charged a duty on each barrel.

beats.scene: A canal boat loaded with barrels of salt glides past tall brick salt works
beats.summary: The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, linked the Hudson River to Lake Erie, and carried salt cheaply from Syracuse to many markets.

beats.scene: Wooden roofs on rollers cover long rows of shallow wooden vats of brine
beats.summary: Syracuse became known as the Salt City, using both boiled and solar methods, with covered vats that were rolled over the brine to keep off the rain.

beats.scene: A river steamer unloads salt barrels beside rows of pork barrels
beats.summary: Salt moved west along the Great Lakes and rivers to farms and meat packers, such as those of Cincinnati, which needed it for pork.

beats.scene: A Confederate quartermaster counts empty salt barrels in a bare warehouse
beats.summary: In the Civil War, the Union blockade cut the South's imports of salt, and prices soared, though salt was needed for meat, leather and horses.

beats.scene: Soldiers in blue and grey coats fight near white salt works
beats.summary: Saltville, Virginia, was the main source of Confederate salt; the Union attacked it in October 1864 and wrecked the works in December.

beats.scene: A southern farm with an empty smokehouse and a family at a bare table
beats.summary: The salt shortage hurt the South's armies and families, and showed that a modern war needed salt as much as guns.

beats.scene: A glassblower and a soap boiler work side by side in a busy street
beats.summary: Industry needed soda ash for glass, soap, paper and cloth, and it came from the ashes of plants.

beats.scene: Scientists in powdered wigs examine a small dish of white powder in a laboratory
beats.summary: In 1783 the French Academy of Sciences offered a prize for a way to make soda from ordinary salt.

beats.scene: A French surgeon in a plain coat stirs a pot in a small workshop
beats.summary: Nicolas Leblanc, a French doctor and chemist, found a method in the early 1790s that turned salt into soda ash.

beats.scene: A man sits alone in a bare room with a closed factory behind him
beats.summary: Leblanc never profited from his invention: the Revolution seized his works and he died poor in 1806.

beats.scene: Tall chimneys belch smoke over rows of workers' houses in a northern English town
beats.summary: Britain's Leblanc works around Liverpool and St Helens made great amounts of soda, and the industry grew very fast.

beats.scene: Dead trees and a pale sky stand beside a smoking factory
beats.summary: The process gave off clouds of hydrochloric acid gas that killed plants and harmed the health of people nearby.

beats.scene: An inspector in a long coat measures air beside a chimney as owners frown
beats.summary: Britain's Alkali Act of 1863 was one of the first laws to control industrial pollution, and it forced makers to capture most of the gas.

beats.scene: A Belgian chemist in a dark coat studies a tall glass tower of gas
beats.summary: Ernest Solvay of Belgium developed a cleaner and cheaper process using ammonia in the 1860s, which gradually replaced Leblanc's.

beats.scene: A new factory with clean white buildings stands beside brine pipes and a river
beats.summary: Brunner and Mond built a large Solvay works at Northwich in Cheshire in the 1870s, using local brine and limestone.

beats.scene: Electric cables and glowing meters beside tanks of brine in a modern chemical plant
beats.summary: Electricity passed through brine produces chlorine and caustic soda, which are used to make bleach, plastics, paper and clean drinking water.

beats.scene: Indian salt workers rake a pan on a hot coast beneath a British flag
beats.summary: India had made salt on its coasts for thousands of years, and the East India Company took control of its salt trade in the eighteenth century.

beats.scene: A tax clerk stamps a salt ledger beside heaped sacks in an Indian warehouse
beats.summary: Under British rule, salt was heavily taxed, and Indians were forbidden to make or sell it without permission.

beats.scene: Ships from Liverpool unload sacks of white salt on a crowded Indian quayside
beats.summary: Salt from Cheshire was shipped to Bengal, and British policy favoured imports and heavy taxes on local salt.

beats.scene: A long line of guards stands beside a thick thorny hedge across a plain
beats.summary: To stop smuggling, the British built an inland customs line across India, partly formed by a thick, thorny hedge.

beats.scene: A guard on horseback patrols a high hedge as villagers wait at a gate
beats.summary: The hedge was guarded by thousands of men, and anyone moving salt across it could be searched and punished.

beats.scene: A thin hedge crumbles into a field while a government clerk closes a ledger
beats.summary: The customs line was given up around 1879 when salt taxes were made more even, but the salt tax itself continued.

beats.scene: A poor family counts coins beside a small bag of salt at home
beats.summary: The tax was the same for everyone, so poor families paid a much larger share of their income than rich ones.

beats.scene: Indian lawyers in white caps hold a meeting beneath a banner
beats.summary: Indian leaders objected to the salt tax for decades, and the Indian National Congress grew into a mass movement.

beats.scene: Congress delegates raise a flag at midnight in a crowded city square
beats.summary: In January 1930 Congress declared that India should be fully independent, and its leaders looked for a way to begin a campaign.

beats.scene: A thin man in simple cloth sits cross-legged and writes at a low desk
beats.summary: Gandhi chose salt because everyone needed it, the poor were hurt most, and breaking the law needed no violence.

beats.scene: A man writes a letter by lamplight while a young messenger waits
beats.summary: On 2 March 1930 Gandhi wrote to the Viceroy, Lord Irwin, to say he would break the salt law, and Irwin replied coldly.

beats.scene: Seventy-eight men and women in plain cloth stand in rows in a dusty courtyard
beats.summary: Gandhi chose seventy-eight followers from his ashram at Sabarmati near Ahmedabad to walk with him.

beats.scene: A grey-haired man in a loincloth leads walkers out of a gate at dawn
beats.summary: On 12 March 1930, at the age of sixty, Gandhi set out on foot toward the sea, and a crowd followed him.

beats.scene: Walkers with bundles move along a dusty road between fields of cotton
beats.summary: The marchers walked about ten miles a day, through the villages of Gujarat, for twenty-four days.

beats.scene: Villagers sprinkle water and scatter leaves on the road as walkers pass
beats.summary: In each village crowds welcomed the marchers, sprinkled the road with water and listened to Gandhi speak.

beats.scene: A village headman takes off his official badge and hands it over
beats.summary: Many local officials resigned their posts as the march passed through, and the number of followers grew.

beats.scene: Reporters with notebooks and cameras gather beside the dusty road
beats.summary: Newspapers in India and abroad reported the march daily, so the world watched Gandhi's slow walk.

beats.scene: British officials in white suits read telegrams around a polished table
beats.summary: British officials were uncertain how to respond, and some thought the plan foolish; the Viceroy hesitated to arrest him.

beats.scene: Tired walkers reach a village beside a wide stretch of sea and mud flats
beats.summary: On 5 April 1930 the marchers reached Dandi, a village on the shore of the Arabian Sea.

beats.scene: A man bends to pick up salty mud on a beach while crowds watch
beats.summary: On the morning of 6 April, Gandhi bathed in the sea, then picked up a lump of natural salt from the beach, breaking the law.

beats.scene: Crowds on a Mumbai beach scoop sea water into pans and wave salt packets
beats.summary: After Dandi, people across India made salt from seawater and sold it openly, defying the law.

beats.scene: Police vans stand outside a crowded prison gate as families wave from the road
beats.summary: Tens of thousands of people were arrested in the campaign, including many women, and the jails filled up.

beats.scene: Police at night enter a mango grove where a thin man sleeps
beats.summary: In the early hours of 5 May 1930, Gandhi was arrested without trial, and held in Yerwada jail near Pune.

beats.scene: Hundreds of volunteers in white march across flat ground toward a fenced salt works
beats.summary: The poet Sarojini Naidu led about two and a half thousand volunteers to the Dharasana Salt Works on 21 May 1930.

beats.scene: Men with long wooden batons stand behind a wire fence as volunteers advance
beats.summary: Police with steel-tipped batons struck the volunteers, who did not defend themselves, and wave after wave came forward.

beats.scene: An American reporter writes notes on his knee beside a stretcher
beats.summary: The American reporter Webb Miller described the scene, and his report, printed in many newspapers, shocked readers around the world.

beats.scene: Officials in a London committee room look at newspapers spread across a long table
beats.summary: Britain's government grew uncomfortable, and the Viceroy decided to open talks, releasing Gandhi in January 1931.

beats.scene: Two men in simple dress shake hands in a grand room under chandeliers
beats.summary: In March 1931 the Gandhi–Irwin Pact released many prisoners and let people living near the coast make salt for their own use.

beats.scene: Calendar pages blow away beside a quiet spinning wheel and a prison door
beats.summary: Freedom did not come at once: more campaigns, imprisonments and a world war followed before independence.

beats.scene: People wave flags and cheer as a new flag is raised in Delhi
beats.summary: On 15 August 1947 India became independent, and the old salt tax was removed soon after, ending a long grievance.

beats.scene: A cook seals glass jars of fruit with wax while soldiers wait outside
beats.summary: In the early 1800s, canning in sealed jars and tin cans began to keep food safe without salt.

beats.scene: A railway wagon with thick walls is loaded with sides of meat
beats.summary: From the 1870s, machines made cold air, and refrigerated trains and ships began to carry fresh meat over long distances.

beats.scene: A family opens a white refrigerator in a bright kitchen beside a salt jar
beats.summary: In the twentieth century, refrigerators in homes and shops made salted food much less necessary for survival.

beats.scene: A deli counter displays ham, cheese, anchovies and pickles beside jars of olives
beats.summary: Salt still gives taste to ham, cheese, anchovies and pickles, so many salted foods remain popular though not essential.

beats.scene: A doctor in an old coat examines the swollen neck of a young woman
beats.summary: In inland and mountain regions, where food had little iodine, many people suffered from goitre, a swelling of the neck.

beats.scene: Schoolgirls in white aprons line up beside a nurse with a tray
beats.summary: In Ohio in the early 1920s, the doctor David Marine tested iodine on schoolgirls and found that it greatly reduced goitre.

beats.scene: A packet of salt with an iodine label stands beside a Swiss mountain village
beats.summary: The answer was iodised salt: Switzerland began selling it in 1922, and the United States followed in 1924.

beats.scene: A mother feeds a baby beside a salt packet with a blue label
beats.summary: Iodised salt works because everyone eats a little every day; it cost little, and did not change the taste.

beats.scene: A child eats breakfast while a mother holds a packet of salt marked iodine
beats.summary: Today most countries add iodine to salt, though some regions still lack it; the history shows salt serving health.

beats.scene: A person reads a food label beside a spoon and packaged meals
beats.summary: Many people now eat more salt than they need, and a high intake is linked with high blood pressure; most comes from packaged food.

beats.scene: Giant white piles of salt rise beside rows of pale evaporating ponds
beats.summary: Today the world makes hundreds of millions of tonnes of salt a year, from solar ponds, mines and wells.

beats.scene: A tanker lorry fills a chemical works beside a small bag of salt
beats.summary: Only a small part of this salt is eaten; most goes to chemical factories, water treatment and roads.

beats.scene: A truck spreads salt on an icy road in winter
beats.summary: Salt is spread on icy roads because it lowers the freezing point of water, but the run-off can harm rivers and soil.

beats.scene: A vast white salt flat reflects the sky as a single jeep crosses it
beats.summary: Salt flats such as the Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia hold brine rich in lithium, which is used in batteries.

beats.scene: Four jars of salt in different textures stand on a kitchen counter
beats.summary: Sea salt, rock salt and table salt are chemically almost the same, mostly sodium chloride, and differ mainly in texture and taste.

beats.scene: A supermarket shelf of cheap salt packets stands beside rows of spice jars
beats.summary: Salt lost its political power when it became cheap, thanks to railways, steamships and mining.

beats.scene: A smiling shop assistant weighs a bag of salt beside a handwritten price tag
beats.summary: In many countries a kilogram of salt now costs about as much as a bus ticket, a sign of how cheap it has become.

beats.scene: A teacher points to idioms on a blackboard in a bright classroom
beats.summary: Our language still carries salt: salary, salad, worth your salt, salt of the earth, and take it with a grain of salt.

beats.scene: A single salt crystal sparkles on a fingertip above a map
beats.summary: A grain of salt has a long journey behind it: an ancient sea, a mine or pond, ships, factories, shops and a table.

beats.scene: A family eats dinner around a table with a salt shaker in the centre
beats.summary: Closing: salt shaped roads, cities, taxes, wars and freedom, and the shaker on the table holds that history.

A town near Naples was famous for its garum.

The city of Timbuktu grew rich from the salt and gold trade.
A story says that salt was sold for its weight in gold.

In Ethiopia, the Afar people still cut salt in the desert.
The Maya people made salt on the coast and traded it.
The Aztecs took salt from lakes and sold it in markets.
In Peru, families still collect salt from pools on a mountain.
In North America, many peoples gathered salt at salty springs.
On the high plateau of Tibet, people carried salt on big animals.
In Japan, people made salt from sea water on sandy beaches.
In some countries, a host welcomes guests with bread and salt.
Eating someone's salt means that you owe them your loyalty.
In holy books, salt can stand for a lasting promise.
In Japan, sumo wrestlers throw salt into the ring before a match.
The German town of Lüneburg had salty springs and made much salt.
The salt works at Lüneburg burned a great deal of wood.
A road called the Old Salt Road went from Lüneburg to the Baltic Sea.
Fishermen caught so many herring that they could not eat them all.
Herring were packed in barrels with layers of salt.
The Hanseatic League was a group of northern trading towns.
Cheap sea salt from France was carried to the north by ship.
Dutch fishermen salted their herring on the ship, at sea.
The city of Venice grew rich by making and selling salt.
Venice guarded its salt trade, and sometimes it fought wars for it.
Near Krakow, in Poland, miners dug salt at a mine called Wieliczka.
The Polish kings earned a lot of money from salt.
The mine was very deep, and horses worked underground too.
Miners carved holy places and statues out of salt.
A legend says a princess lost a ring that was found in the salt.
Boats with salt moved on the river Salzach in Austria.
In 1611, soldiers from Bavaria took the city of Salzburg.
A famous old English book of 1086 lists salt houses.

In 1670, people found a thick bed of rock salt in Cheshire.
The kings of France made a tax on salt, called the gabelle.
People in some parts of France paid much more for salt than others.
Families had to buy a set amount of salt each year.
Guards searched carts and houses to look for illegal salt.
Some people carried salt secretly at night to sell it for more money.

In the French Revolution, people demanded the end of the gabelle.
Napoleon brought back a salt tax in 1806.
In 1646, Russia put a heavy tax on salt, and prices went up.
In 1648, an angry crowd marched through the streets of Moscow.
Sailors ate salted meat from barrels on long trips across the sea.
Sailors called the hard salty meat salt horse.
Explorers took salted food on their ships to cross the ocean.
Sailors who ate no fresh fruit often became sick.
Basque fishermen sailed far out into the Atlantic to catch cod.
Cod was split open, salted and dried in the sun.
People ate salt cod on days when the church did not allow meat.
The cheapest salted fish was sent to the Caribbean islands.
On the Turks Islands, workers pulled salt from shallow ponds.
Enslaved people did the hard work on the salt islands.
During the war, British ships stopped salt from reaching America.
People along the coast boiled sea water to make their own salt.
The Onondaga people had long used salt springs near their lake.
Settlers boiled the salty water, and New York State collected a tax.
The Erie Canal opened in 1825 and carried salt on boats.
Syracuse became known as the Salt City.
Boats carried salt west to farms and meat packers.

Soldiers fought for control of the salt works at Saltville.
Without enough salt, many families in the South went hungry.

Two Englishmen built a large new factory in Cheshire in the 1870s.

B1B2: A pinch of salt seems like the smallest thing in the kitchen. Yet for thousands of years it has built cities, moved caravans and started wars.
Salt is a joining of two elements, sodium and chlorine. Look at a grain through a lens and you will see that it is a tiny cube.
Every nerve in your body uses salt to carry its tiny electrical signals. Your muscles, including your heart, also need it to work properly.
When we work in the heat, we lose water and salt through our sweat. If you ever taste your own skin after a long run, you will notice that it is salty.
Tears, blood and sweat all taste salty, because the fluids inside us contain salt. Our bodies work hard to keep that amount steady, a little like a small sea carried inside the skin.
The human body cannot make salt, so we have to take it from the outside. That simple fact has pushed people to search for salt in every age.
If the body runs very low on salt, a person can feel weak and dizzy and get painful muscle cramps. In serious cases the person may become confused and need a doctor.
Cows, deer and children all enjoy a salty taste, because the tongue is built to notice salt. Farmers still set out blocks of salt for their cattle to lick.
A healthy adult needs only a small amount of salt each day, far less than most people eat today. In the past, though, even that small amount was hard to find.
In this book we will follow salt through deserts, seas, mines and market squares. Along the way we will meet camels, kings, tax collectors, smugglers and one famous walker.
Seawater tastes salty because it holds a great deal of dissolved salt. About three and a half parts in every hundred are salts, and most of that is the ordinary kind.
Some lakes in dry lands have rivers flowing in but none flowing out. The sun dries the water away, so the salt stays behind and the lake becomes saltier every year.
Rain that sinks deep into the ground may flow past buried beds of salt. When it comes back up in a spring, the water is already full of salt, and people call it brine.
Long ago, shallow seas dried up and left thick layers of salt on their beds. Later, sand and clay covered the salt and kept it safe underground for millions of years.
Rock salt is lighter than the rock above it, and under great pressure it can flow very slowly. Over millions of years it can push upward in a great dome, which is easier for miners to reach.
Deer, cattle and other animals will travel a long way to a salt lick, a patch of salty earth. Over many years their hooves wear deep paths through the forest.
Early hunters probably found many salt licks simply by following the animals. A good lick was a good place to wait for meat, so people came back to it year after year.
A hunting people who eat plenty of meat and blood may get enough salt from their food. Many hunters, in fact, did not add salt to their meals at all.
Early farmers ate mostly grain and vegetables, which hold very little salt. Many scholars think this is why farming peoples began adding salt to their meals and trading for it.
In Romania, scientists have found clay pots and ash beside a salty spring. They think that people boiled brine there about eight thousand years ago, which makes it one of the oldest salt works known.
Salt draws water out of food, and without water the germs that make food rot cannot grow. That is why a salted fish can last for months instead of days.
Fishermen split their catch, rubbed salt into the flesh and left the fish to dry in the wind. A fish treated like this could travel far from the sea and still be good to eat.
Pork can be rubbed with salt and hung up to become ham, or packed in barrels as salt pork. Both lasted far longer than fresh meat, and the old methods are still used today.
Olives taste bitter when they are picked, and soaking them in brine makes them pleasant to eat. Some cheeses, such as the Greek feta, are also stored in brine so that they keep.
When cabbage is packed with salt, friendly bacteria start to work on it. In a few weeks it turns into sauerkraut or kimchi, which are sour, tasty and safe to keep.
Soy sauce and miso begin with cooked beans, grain and plenty of salt. The mixture is left in big barrels for months while tiny living things slowly change its flavour.
Salt does more than keep food from spoiling, because it also brings out flavour. A loaf of bread without salt tastes dull, and many cooks say that a dish without it is unfinished.
In many parts of Europe, farmers killed their pigs in late autumn, because the animals could not be fed through the winter. They salted the meat at once, and it fed the family until spring.
Salted food does not spoil quickly, so travellers, soldiers and sailors could carry it for weeks. Without salt, long journeys and large armies would have been much harder to feed.
Whoever controlled the salt also controlled the food supply, and that gave them real power. This is why kings, priests and merchants all wanted to own it.
In warm, sunny places, people let seawater flow into wide, shallow ponds. The sun and the wind slowly dried the water away, and a crust of white salt was left behind.
At Guérande, on the coast of France, workers have gathered salt for more than a thousand years. They pull the crystals into small heaps with long wooden rakes, much as their ancestors did.
In cold, wet countries the sun was too weak to dry the brine, so people boiled it in pots and pans over a fire. It was slow work, and it needed a huge amount of wood.
A salt works could burn a whole forest, and in some places the wood cost more than the workers did. Later, cheap coal helped to ease this problem, but it brought troubles of its own.
Miners cut great rooms in the salt bed and left thick pillars of salt standing to hold up the roof. This clever method is called room-and-pillar mining, and it is still in use today.
High in the Austrian Alps lies Hallstatt, where people dug for salt more than three thousand years ago. The mine made the region rich, and the nearby city of Salzburg is named for salt.

Because salt keeps things from rotting, old clothes, leather and wooden tools have survived in the Hallstatt mine. Scientists have even studied scraps of food left by the miners, and these tell us what they ate.
Near the mines, archaeologists have found graves full of fine objects, some from lands far away. Scholars believe that the salt trade paid for them, and the period is now named after Hallstatt.
In modern times, a salt company may drill a well and pump fresh water down into a salt bed. The water dissolves the salt, and the brine is then pumped back up to the surface.
Modern factories boil brine in sealed vessels from which the air has been pumped out. Under low pressure the water boils at a lower heat, so much less fuel is needed than in the old open pans.
In Sichuan, in western China, a great deal of salty water lies far under the ground. More than two thousand years ago, people began to drill wells to reach it.
A heavy iron bit hung from a strong bamboo cable above the hole. Workers jumped on a wooden lever to lift it, and then the bit fell and broke the rock below it.
As the centuries passed, the wells of Sichuan grew deeper and deeper. A well finished in 1835 reached about a thousand metres, and its builders worked on it for more than ten years.
The brine had to be lifted up from deep underground. Water buffalo walked round a great wooden drum, which wound up a long bamboo tube full of salty water.
Sometimes the drillers struck natural gas instead of brine. Clever workers carried it through bamboo pipes to burn under their pans, so they could boil brine without cutting any wood.
About two thousand years ago, the Han emperors took control of salt and iron. Only the state's own workers and merchants were allowed to make and sell them.
In 81 BCE, officials and scholars met at court to argue about the salt and iron monopoly. Officials said it paid for defence, but scholars said it made life harder for the poor.
Rulers in many lands liked to tax salt, and the reasons were simple. Everyone needed it, only a few places made it, and officials could easily watch the people who sold it.
In China, the money from salt paid for armies, roads and canals. At some times in history, historians say, salt made up a very large share of what the government earned.
Merchants who held a licence to sell salt could become very rich. In the Chinese city of Yangzhou, for example, some of them built beautiful gardens and supported painters and writers.
In the Egyptian desert, some lakes dry up in summer and leave a pale crust behind. This crust is natron, a mineral that contains salt and other useful substances.
To make a mummy, Egyptian priests covered the body with natron and left it for about forty days. After that, the dry body was washed, oiled and wrapped in fine linen.
A dry body does not rot, for the same reason that salted fish does not rot. Without water, the germs that cause decay cannot live.
The Nile was full of fish, and the Egyptians dried and salted what they could not eat at once. Salted fish and birds were cheap food for the workers in the cities.
Natron was useful for more than preserving the dead. Egyptians used it for cleaning their bodies and their clothes, and later it became an ingredient in glass.
In ancient Mesopotamia, farmers watered their fields from canals, and salt in the ground slowly rose to the surface. Some scholars think this harmed their wheat and made the soil harder to farm.
The Dead Sea is many times saltier than the ocean, so no fish can live in it. Its old Hebrew name means the Salt Sea, and people have gathered its salt for thousands of years.
The Phoenicians, who lived in cities such as Tyre and Sidon, were great sea traders. They probably carried salt and salted fish to harbours all around the Mediterranean.
The Greek cities did not have enough land to feed everyone, so they imported food. Athens, for example, bought salted fish and grain from the lands around the Black Sea.
The Greek poet Homer called salt divine, which shows how highly the Greeks valued it. Salt was also used in religious customs, and the Romans sprinkled flour and salt on animals offered to the gods.
Not far from Rome, where the river Tiber meets the sea, workers made salt in shallow pans. An old tradition says that the port of Ostia was founded to guard them.
The Via Salaria, or Salt Road, is older than Rome itself. Traders from the hills used it to carry salt up from the coast to the towns of the interior.
The Roman government wanted to control salt and its price. According to the writer Livy, one official taxed salt in 204 BCE and was nicknamed Salinator, the Salt Man.
The English word salary comes from the Latin word salarium. Some Roman writers said it meant money given to soldiers to buy salt, though modern scholars are not sure.
Many English words come from sal, the Latin word for salt. Salad, sauce and sausage all began as things that were seasoned or preserved with salt.
Around the empire, along the coasts of Spain and North Africa, there were large factories for salting fish. They sent their products by ship to cities all over the Roman world.
To make garum, workers layered small fish and fish parts with salt in big stone tanks. The mixture stood in the sun for weeks, and then the liquid was drawn off as sauce.
The city of Pompeii, which was buried by a volcano in the year 79, was famous for its garum. Archaeologists have found jars there that still carry the names of the makers.
The Roman farmer and writer Cato wrote a handbook with advice on salting hams. Salting meat was an ordinary job on any farm, and every farmer needed a good supply of salt.
When the Romans conquered Britain, they also made salt there. At Droitwich they boiled brine in pans, and some old roads there are still called salt ways.
In West Africa, the southern lands had gold but little salt. The Sahara desert in the north had plenty of salt, so each side wanted what the other one had.
Camels came to North Africa about two thousand years ago, and they changed the desert trade. They could cross the Sahara carrying salt to the south and bringing back gold.
In 1352 the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta reached Taghaza, a desert town in the Sahara. He wrote that its houses and even its mosque were built from slabs of salt and roofed with camel skins.
Ibn Battuta did not enjoy his stay at Taghaza. He found the water bad and the place unpleasant, and he noted that the workers lived by digging salt and trading it.
Workers cut the salt into large slabs, and each camel carried two of them, one on each side. The caravans then travelled for weeks across the sand to the markets in the south.
After some years, the mines of Taghaza ran low, and the mines at Taoudenni took their place. Even today, a few caravans still carry salt across the desert by camel.
Timbuktu stood where the desert met the lands of the south, so it became a great meeting place for merchants. The city grew rich, and it also became a famous centre of learning.
A famous story says that salt was once traded for its weight in gold. Historians doubt that this was often true, but both goods were valuable and the rulers taxed them both.
In the highlands of Ethiopia, flat bars of salt called amole were used as small coins. People kept using them until the twentieth century, and they could be broken into pieces.
In the Danakil Depression of Ethiopia, the Afar people still cut salt by hand from a flat white plain. It is one of the hottest places on Earth, but the work goes on.
The Maya lived in Central America, and they made salt along the coast. Archaeologists have found the remains of salt works in Belize, where workers boiled brine in clay pots.
The Aztecs lived beside shallow salty lakes, and they gathered the salt from them. They sold it in the big markets of their capital, and they also honoured a goddess of salt.
High in the Andes, at a place called Maras, hundreds of little pools are cut into the hillside. A warm salty spring fills them, and families collect the salt when the water dries.
Long before Europeans arrived, the peoples of North America gathered salt at springs and licks. They also traded it, sometimes over very long distances.
The high plateau of Tibet has many salt lakes, and herders carried the salt by yak to farmers in the valleys. The farmers gave them grain in return, and Tibetans still add salt to their butter tea.
Japan has almost no rock salt or salt lakes, so its people made salt from the sea. They poured seawater on sand, collected the salty sand and boiled the strong brine.
In Russia and many other lands, a host may welcome an important guest with a round loaf and a little dish of salt. It is a sign of friendship, and it shows that the guest is respected and welcome.
In many cultures, if you have eaten a person's salt, you owe that person loyalty. In Urdu and Hindi, a faithful friend is called namak halal, which means true to the salt.
The Hebrew Bible speaks of a covenant of salt, which means a promise that lasts. The Gospel of Matthew says to believers, you are the salt of the earth.
In Japan, salt is a symbol of purity in the Shinto religion. Sumo wrestlers throw a handful into the ring before a match, and some shops put small piles by their doors.
The German town of Lüneburg stood above a bed of salt, and its springs had been used for more than a thousand years. The town became very rich from the salt that was boiled there.
Boiling brine took an enormous quantity of wood, and the forests around Lüneburg slowly shrank. The works also needed lead for the pans and many workers to keep the fires burning.
The Old Salt Road ran from Lüneburg to Lübeck, a port on the Baltic Sea. Carts loaded with salt barrels travelled along it for days, and inns and little towns grew up beside it.
In autumn, enormous schools of herring came to the sea near southern Sweden. The fishermen could catch more than anyone could eat, so they needed a lot of salt to keep the fish.
Workers cleaned each herring quickly and packed it in a barrel in layers of salt. The full barrels were then sent by ship and cart to towns and monasteries across Europe.
The Hanseatic League was a group of trading towns in northern Europe, and Lübeck was its leader. The towns protected one another's ships and became rich selling salt, fish and grain.
Salt made by the sun in western France was cheaper than the boiled salt of Lüneburg. Dutch ships carried this sea salt, called bay salt, to the northern fishing ports.
Dutch fishermen cleaned and salted their herring on board their ships at sea. A legend says a man called Beukelszoon invented the method, but nobody knows if he really did.
Venice built much of its power on the sale of salt, which it made in its own lagoon. The city also bought more from other places and sold it across northern Italy.
Venice kept strict control of its salt trade and had a special office to manage it. It even went to war with neighbouring Ferrara in the 1480s partly because of disputes over salt.
Near the Polish city of Krakow lies Wieliczka, a salt mine worked since the thirteenth century. Over about seven hundred years, miners dug out a whole world of tunnels and halls.
The mines at Wieliczka and Bochnia belonged to the king of Poland. The money from their salt paid for the royal court, for castles and for part of the army.
The mine at Wieliczka reached about three hundred metres below the ground. Miners went down in baskets, and horses were lowered into the tunnels to pull the heavy loads of salt.
Over the years, miners carved chapels, altars and statues out of the walls of the mine. The biggest is the Chapel of Saint Kinga, which has chandeliers made of salt crystals.
A legend tells of Princess Kinga, who threw her ring into a salt mine in Hungary before she left for Poland. When miners in Wieliczka cut into the salt, they found it.
The Austrian city of Salzburg takes its name from the salt barges that once travelled on the river Salzach. Salt from nearby mines made its rulers, the archbishops, very rich.
In 1611 Bavaria and Salzburg quarrelled over the salt trade, and soldiers from Bavaria invaded the city. The archbishop, Wolf Dietrich, lost his power and was put in prison.
The English Domesday Book of 1086 listed the salt houses of the Cheshire towns Nantwich, Northwich and Middlewich. The ending wich in their names comes from an old word for a salt works.
For hundreds of years, workers in Cheshire boiled brine in large pans in smoky buildings. Packhorses and carts then carried the white salt to towns all over England.
In 1670, people looking for coal near Northwich found a thick bed of rock salt instead. Later, the river Weaver was made deeper so that boats could carry the salt away.
In the fourteenth century, the kings of France began to tax salt, and the tax was called the gabelle. Kings needed money for wars, and nobody could live without salt.
The gabelle was not the same in every part of the country. People in some regions paid very high prices for salt, while people in other regions, such as Brittany, paid very little.
In the high-tax regions, each household had to buy a fixed amount of salt every year. It did not matter if the family needed it or not, and they had to pay the full price.
The French crown hired tax farmers, who paid for the right to collect the gabelle. Their guards had the right to search carts and houses for salt that had not been taxed.

Because salt was cheap in Brittany and dear elsewhere, smugglers bought it in the cheap regions and carried it secretly across the border at night. They sold it in the expensive regions and made a very good profit.
The punishment for smuggling salt could be very severe, even for poor people. A smuggler might pay a heavy fine, go to prison or be sent to the galleys, where convicts had to row the king's warships.
When the French Revolution began in 1789, many people wrote lists of complaints, and the gabelle was near the top. In 1790 the new government abolished the tax at last.
Salt remained far too useful for governments ever to forget about it. In 1806 Napoleon brought back a salt tax to raise money for his wars, and in France it lasted until 1945.
In 1646 the Russian government put a heavy tax on salt, and the price rose sharply. Many people could not afford enough salt, and fish rotted before it could be preserved.
In 1648 an angry crowd marched through the streets of Moscow, and the event is known as the Salt Riot. The people attacked the house of Morozov, and the young tsar was forced to send him away.
Ships on long voyages could not carry fresh meat, so sailors ate beef and pork preserved in salt. The meat was packed in barrels and stored below the deck.
Sailors had a joking name for their salted beef, which they called salt horse. It was so hard and salty that the cook had to soak it in water before he could cook it.
Explorers such as Columbus and Magellan took salted meat and fish with them across the oceans. Without salted food, these journeys of many months would not have been possible.
A diet of salted meat and ship's biscuit has almost no fresh fruit, and many sailors became ill with a disease called scurvy. The cure, citrus fruit, was not widely used until the eighteenth century.

The Basques, from the north of Spain, were bold fishermen who sailed far out into the Atlantic for cod. Some historians think they may have reached Newfoundland even before Columbus, but others disagree.
Fishermen in Newfoundland had two main ways of preparing their catch. They could salt the cod on board their ships, or they could split it, salt it and dry it on wooden racks on the shore.
In Catholic countries, the Church did not allow meat on fast days such as Fridays and in Lent. Salted cod was a cheap and popular choice, and in Spain and Portugal people still love it.
The cheapest salted cod was sent to the islands of the Caribbean. There it was used to feed enslaved people who worked on sugar plantations, and it was part of a very cruel system.
On the Turks Islands, in the Caribbean, shallow ponds filled with seawater in the rainy season. The sun dried them, and workers raked the salt, which ships carried to North America.

The work on the Turks Islands was done by enslaved Africans who raked salt for long hours under a burning sun. Salt and sunlight caused painful sores on their skin, and slavery in the British Empire was abolished only in 1834.
Before the American Revolution, most salt in the colonies came from overseas. When war began, British warships blocked the harbours, and the American army struggled to keep its meat from spoiling.
Many Americans tried to make their own salt by boiling seawater in kettles along the coast. Some state governments even offered rewards to anyone who built a successful salt works.
In central New York, the Onondaga people had used the salt springs by their lake for centuries. A French priest wrote about them in 1654, which was the first time Europeans described them in print.
After the Revolution, settlers began to boil the springs' brine in iron kettles and sell the salt. The State of New York owned the springs and charged a small tax on every barrel.

The Erie Canal, which opened in 1825, joined the Hudson River to Lake Erie across about three hundred and sixty miles. Boats could carry heavy barrels of salt cheaply along it, and a small tax on salt helped to pay for it.
Syracuse grew into a busy town known as the Salt City. Some brine was boiled, and some was dried by the sun in long vats with roofs that rolled over them when it rained.
Boats and canals carried the salt west to the Great Lakes and the Ohio River. Farmers and meat packers in places such as Cincinnati needed huge quantities of salt for their pork.
In the American Civil War, the Union navy blocked the ports of the South and cut off its imports of salt. Prices soared, and the Confederate army and civilians struggled to find enough.
The biggest salt works in the South were at Saltville, in Virginia, and they were guarded closely. The Union attacked them in October 1864 and failed, but it returned in December and wrecked them.
The lack of salt hurt the South's armies and its families, and it made the war harder to bear. It showed that a modern war needed salt almost as much as it needed guns.
As factories spread, they needed soda ash for making glass, soap, paper and cloth. For a long time it came from burnt plants, and the supply could not keep pace with demand.
In 1783 the French Academy of Sciences offered a prize for a way to make soda from ordinary salt. Salt was cheap and plentiful, so the idea was very attractive.
A French doctor and chemist named Nicolas Leblanc found a method in the early 1790s. His process turned ordinary salt into soda ash with the help of acid, limestone and coal.
Sadly, Leblanc never made any money from his clever invention. The Revolution took his factory, and he died in poverty in 1806 without ever winning the prize.

In the nineteenth century, large factories in northern England, near Liverpool and St Helens, made huge quantities of soda ash. They used Cheshire salt, and the region became a great centre of chemistry.
The Leblanc process gave off clouds of hydrochloric acid gas. The gas killed trees and crops for miles around, and local people complained that it harmed their health.
In 1863, the British Parliament passed the Alkali Act, which is often called one of the first laws against industrial pollution. It forced the factories to capture most of their dangerous gas.
In the 1860s, a Belgian chemist named Ernest Solvay developed a new process that used ammonia. It was cleaner and cheaper than Leblanc's, and it gradually replaced the older method.
In the 1870s, two English partners, Brunner and Mond, built a large factory at Northwich in Cheshire. It used local brine and limestone to make soda ash by the Solvay method.

Later, engineers discovered that an electric current passed through brine splits it into new substances. These include chlorine and caustic soda, which are used for making bleach, paper, plastics and clean drinking water.
India's long coasts and dry plains had given its people salt for thousands of years. In the late eighteenth century, the East India Company took control of the salt trade in Bengal.
Under British rule, salt was heavily taxed, and the government controlled its sale. Indian families were forbidden to make or sell salt without permission, even though the sea was right beside them.
For many years, British merchants shipped Cheshire salt to Bengal. Heavy taxes on Indian salt made the English salt cheaper, so the local salt-makers lost much of their trade.
To stop salt from being smuggled, the British built a huge customs line across India. In many places it was made of thorny bushes planted close together, and thousands of guards watched it.
Guards watched the hedge day and night, and they searched travellers at the gates. Anyone found carrying salt without a tax stamp could be punished.

In about 1879, the British brought the salt taxes of different regions closer together, and the customs line was no longer needed. The hedge was gradually forgotten, but the salt tax itself continued.
The salt tax was the same for everyone, rich or poor. A poor family, however, had to spend a far larger share of its small income on it.
For many years, Indian leaders spoke against the salt tax, and many people agreed with them. The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, grew into a large movement that wanted self-government.
In January 1930 the Indian National Congress declared that India should be completely independent. Its leaders then had to decide how to begin a campaign, and many ideas were suggested.
Gandhi chose salt because everyone needed it and the poor were hurt most by the tax. Breaking the salt law also needed no weapons, only the act of picking up salt.
On 2 March 1930 Gandhi wrote a long letter to the Viceroy, Lord Irwin. He explained why the salt tax was unjust and said that he would break the salt law unless something changed.
Gandhi lived in a community called an ashram, at Sabarmati near the city of Ahmedabad. He chose seventy-eight people from it, young and old, to walk with him.
On the morning of 12 March 1930, after prayers, Gandhi set out on foot toward the sea. He was sixty years old, and a large crowd came to see him leave.
The marchers walked about ten miles a day, starting early each morning before the heat grew strong. The whole journey was about two hundred and forty miles, and it took twenty-four days.
In each village, crowds came out to welcome the walkers. They watered the dusty road, scattered leaves and flowers on it, and listened to Gandhi speak in the evening.
As the march went on, many local officials resigned from their government posts in support of it. Each day, more people joined the line, and the group became larger and larger.
Journalists from India and other countries followed the march, and newspapers wrote about it every day. Soon people across the world knew about the old man who was walking to the sea.
British officials argued among themselves about how to respond. Some thought the plan was foolish, and the Viceroy hesitated to arrest Gandhi because he did not want to make him a hero.
On 5 April 1930 the marchers arrived at Dandi, a small village on the coast of the Arabian Sea. They had walked for twenty-four days, and a very large crowd was waiting.
On the morning of 6 April 1930, Gandhi bathed in the sea. Then he walked to the beach, bent down and picked up a lump of natural salt, and in doing so he broke the law.
After Dandi, people all over India began to make salt in defiance of the law. They boiled seawater on the shore and sold small packets of salt in the streets of the big cities.
The British arrested tens of thousands of people for breaking the salt laws. Many women took part in the protests, and soon the prisons were full.
In the early hours of 5 May 1930, police arrived at the place where Gandhi was staying and arrested him. He was held in prison at Yerwada, near the city of Pune, without a trial.
