On 21 May 1930, the poet and leader Sarojini Naidu led a large group of volunteers to the Dharasana Salt Works. There were perhaps two and a half thousand of them, and they planned to take the salt peacefully.

Police with long steel-tipped sticks waited at the gates, and they struck the volunteers as they came forward. The volunteers did not fight back, and new waves of people kept walking toward the police.
An American reporter named Webb Miller watched the events and described them in great detail. His report was printed in many newspapers, and it shocked people all over the world.
The British government felt embarrassed by the stories in the newspapers. By the start of 1931, the Viceroy decided to talk with Gandhi, and he released him from prison in January.
In March 1931, Gandhi and Lord Irwin signed an agreement called the Gandhi–Irwin Pact. It released many prisoners, and it allowed people living near the coast to make salt for their own use.

Freedom did not come immediately, and the struggle was far from over. The struggle went on for many more years, with new campaigns, more arrests and the Second World War, which brought great changes to Britain's empire.
On 15 August 1947, India finally became an independent country after a long struggle. The salt tax that had caused so much anger was removed soon after, and nobody had to pay it again.
In the early 1800s, a Frenchman named Nicolas Appert showed that food heated in sealed jars did not spoil. Soon afterward, the idea was used with tin cans, and it did not need salt.

From the 1870s, engineers built machines that made cold air. Trains and ships with refrigerated rooms could now carry fresh meat over long distances, and in 1882 a frozen cargo reached Britain from New Zealand.
In the twentieth century, refrigerators became common in homes and shops. Fresh food could now be kept cold for days, so people no longer depended on salted food in winter.
Salted foods did not disappear, because many people simply like them. Ham, bacon, cheese, anchovies and pickles are still loved, and now it is the taste that matters, not the need.
Some people who lived far from the sea, in mountain valleys, developed a large swelling in the neck called a goitre. It happens when the body does not get enough of a mineral called iodine.
Between 1917 and 1922, a doctor named David Marine ran a large test in Ohio. Schoolgirls who were given iodine developed far less goitre than girls who were not, and so the answer was clear.
The answer was to add a very small amount of iodine to table salt. Switzerland began to sell iodised salt in 1922, and the United States followed in 1924.
Iodised salt works because nearly everybody eats a little salt every day. The iodine costs very little, and it does not change the taste, so people hardly notice it.
Today, many countries encourage or require the use of iodised salt. In a few places people still do not get enough iodine, and health workers there are trying to reach them.
Today many people eat more salt than they need. A high intake is linked with high blood pressure, and most of the salt in many people's diets comes from packaged food and restaurant meals.

Today, the world makes more than two hundred million tonnes of salt every year. It comes from sunny ponds, from underground mines and from wells, and China, India and the United States are among the biggest makers.
Only a small part of the salt we make is eaten. Most of it goes to chemical factories, to water treatment and to roads, and some of it is also used for feeding farm animals.
In winter, trucks spread salt on icy roads, because salt makes ice melt at a lower temperature. This keeps travellers safer, but the salty run-off can harm rivers, soil and even cars.
In Bolivia, the Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat in the world. Under its white crust lies brine that is rich in lithium, which is a metal used in batteries for phones and cars.
Sea salt, rock salt and fine table salt are all mostly sodium chloride. They differ mainly in the size of their grains, in the tiny amounts of other minerals and in the way they feel and taste.
Salt lost its power when it became cheap and easy to get. Railways, steamships and modern mines delivered it everywhere, and nobody had to go to war over it any more.
In many countries, a large bag of salt now costs only a few coins. It is one of the cheapest things in the shop, and nobody thinks of locking it up.
Our language still remembers salt in a great many everyday ways. We say that a good worker is worth their salt, and we take a doubtful story with a pinch of salt.
A single grain of salt may have begun in an ancient sea, then lain underground for millions of years. A miner or a pond worker brought it up, and a lorry or ship took it to a shop.
Salt marked out roads, built cities, filled the treasuries of kings and helped to start wars and protests. The next time you pick up the salt shaker, remember how much history is inside it.
C1C2: A grain of salt is so small that we hardly notice it, and so common that most of us never wonder where it comes from. Yet for thousands of years this humble mineral has decided where cities were built, which roads were travelled and which governments grew rich. This book follows its trail around the world, from ancient pans beside the sea to the shaker on your table.

Chemists call salt sodium chloride, a compound of sodium, a soft metal that reacts fiercely with water, and chlorine, a pale and poisonous gas. Joined together, the two become a calm white crystal that is harmless in small amounts and essential to life. Look at a single grain through a lens and you will find a neat cube, because its atoms stack themselves in orderly rows.

Inside every living body, salt dissolves into charged particles that carry electrical signals along the nerves and make the muscles contract. The beating of the heart, the blink of an eye and the lifting of a hand all depend on this quiet traffic of particles. Without enough salt, the body's delicate wiring would slowly fail, and its owner would feel the effects long before he understood the cause.

A labourer cutting hay under a summer sun can lose a surprising amount of salt through his skin, and a dried white film on his shirt shows where it went. That loss has to be made good from his food and drink, day after day, whatever the season and however poor the household. For most of history, finding enough salt was a real daily problem for working people.

The fluids that bathe our cells, and the blood that carries them, are salty in a way that quietly recalls the sea. The kidneys keep the balance with great care, saving salt when it is scarce and sending the extra away when there is too much. Few of us notice this steady work, yet it goes on every minute of our lives.

Plants can make sugar from sunlight and animals can make fat from food, but no living body can manufacture its own salt. It has to come from outside, from the soil, the sea or the food we eat. That single fact explains why people in every age and place have gone to such lengths to find it.

When the body is badly short of salt, the first signs are tiredness and muscle cramps, and in severe cases a person can become dizzy, confused and dangerously ill. This can happen to athletes who sweat heavily and then drink only plain water for hours. Doctors treat it seriously, but for most people in rich countries today it is rare.

The tongue has special cells that recognise salt, and the pleasure we feel at a salty taste is probably the body's way of telling us to find more. Farmers know this well, and they still leave blocks of salt in the fields for cattle to lick. The same longing, scientists think, once sent our distant ancestors searching across the land.

The amount of salt a healthy person really needs is surprisingly small, a good deal less than the average meal in a rich country provides. That makes the ancient hunger for salt all the more remarkable, since a little goes a long way. Yet when even that little was missing, no one could invent a substitute, and no amount of other food could fill the gap.

In the chapters that follow we will trace salt from the glittering flats of the Sahara to the cold herring ports of the Baltic, and from the bamboo wells of China to the canal boats of New York. We will meet kings who taxed it, smugglers who stole it and an Indian lawyer who turned a handful of it into a weapon. By the end, the shaker beside your plate may seem a little less ordinary.

The oceans are the greatest store of salt on Earth, for every hundred parts of seawater hold about three and a half parts of dissolved salts, most of them the ordinary kind. Rivers have been washing minerals into the sea for millions of years, and the water that evaporates leaves the salt behind. If all the salt in the oceans were spread over the land, it would form a thick white layer.

In dry regions a lake may receive streams and rivers but have no outlet to the sea, so the only way for water to escape is to rise into the sky. The salts brought in by the streams stay behind, and the lake grows steadily saltier, as the Dead Sea and the Great Salt Lake have done. In the hottest part of the year the shores turn white with a crust of salt that people can simply scrape up and carry home.

Where rainwater seeps down and passes through buried layers of salt, it dissolves some of the mineral and carries it along underground. When the water finds a crack and rises to the surface again, it emerges as a spring of brine, ready-made and needing only to be boiled. Such springs were treasured by everyone who lived near them, and whole settlements often grew up around a single source.

Deep below many countries lie beds of rock salt, the remains of shallow seas that dried up many millions of years ago. Wind and rivers then buried them under sand and clay, and the crystals slept undisturbed until miners broke into them. Some of these beds are hundreds of metres thick, and a single one can supply the world for a very long time.

Under heavy pressure, buried salt behaves a little like thick dough, and because it is lighter than the stone around it, it creeps upward through the crust at a pace of a few millimetres a year. The result is a salt dome, a mushroom-shaped plug that may rise almost to the surface and bring the mineral within reach of a miner's shaft. Many of the world's richest deposits, and much of its oil as well, lie in or beside such domes.

Wild animals have always known where to find salt, and herds of deer, cattle and bison will cross many miles of country to reach a salty spring or a patch of mineral earth. Year after year their hooves beat deep tracks through the woods, and some of these paths were later used as roads. The animals were, in a sense, the first surveyors of the salt trade, and they never asked to be paid.

Hunters who tracked their prey probably discovered many salt sources long before anyone thought of digging for them, since a lick was an excellent place to wait for a meal. People returned to such places in every season, and in time the licks became familiar landmarks on the map in their heads. Nobody can say for certain, but the likeliest teachers of salt were the animals themselves.

Fresh meat and blood contain a fair amount of salt, so peoples who lived mainly by hunting often had little need to season their food. Travellers who met such people sometimes reported with surprise that they disliked salt and thought it a strange taste. The demand that would one day move caravans and fleets began with a change in diet, not with hunger alone.

When people settled down to farm, their meals changed from meat to bread, porridge and vegetables, foods that contain very little of the salt the body needs. Many scholars think this change created a steady demand for salt, because a farmer could grow grain but could not grow salt in his field. From that moment on, salt was something to be fetched, bought or traded from somewhere else.

At a salt spring in the Carpathian hills of Romania, archaeologists have found the remains of clay pots, hearths and ash that seem to date from about eight thousand years ago. The people who lived there appear to have boiled the brine until only salt remained, which would make this one of the earliest known salt works. The dating is a matter of study, but the picture is clear enough: salt-making is almost as old as farming itself.

Salt keeps food by pulling moisture out of it, and the bacteria and moulds that cause decay cannot survive without water. A fish or a joint of meat packed in salt can stay edible for months or even years. Before refrigerators, this was the only reliable way to carry a harvest or a catch through the winter.

On shores around the world, fishermen learned to split their catch, pack it in salt and leave it to dry in the sun and wind. Fish treated in this way was light, hard and almost indestructible, so it could be sold in towns hundreds of miles from the sea. For coastal peoples, salted fish was a kind of money that never lost its value.

A leg of pork rubbed thoroughly with salt and hung in a cool place slowly becomes ham, while the rest of the animal might be packed in barrels as salt pork for the winter. Cured meat kept for many months and could be carried on long journeys, so it fed travellers, soldiers and sailors as well as families. The methods are very old, and in many villages around the world they are still followed in much the same way today.

Fresh olives are too bitter to eat straight from the tree, but soaking them in salty water softens the taste and makes them safe to keep for months. In much the same way, certain cheeses are stored in brine, which protects them from spoiling and gives them their sharp, tangy flavour. Both foods were important across the Mediterranean, where salt and olive groves were close neighbours.

When shredded cabbage is pounded with salt and sealed in a crock, the salt draws out the juice and protects the vegetable from the wrong kind of microbes. The friendly bacteria that tolerate salt then go to work, turning the sugars into acid and producing the sour tang of sauerkraut or kimchi. The result keeps for months, and it also supplies vitamins in a season when fresh greens were scarce.

In China, Japan and Korea, cooks learned to ferment cooked soybeans and grain with generous amounts of salt, and the barrels then rested for months or even years. During that time microscopic organisms broke the beans down into the dark, savoury liquid known as soy sauce, or into the thick paste called miso. Without salt to control the process, the whole barrel would simply rot, and the cook would have nothing to show for months of waiting.

Quite apart from its power to preserve, salt makes food taste better, softening bitterness and bringing out sweetness and savour. A loaf baked without it tastes strangely flat, and cooks in every culture have learned that a dish is rarely finished until it has been seasoned. This was a second reason why the demand for salt never fell, even in the years of plenty.

In many parts of Europe, the autumn slaughter was one of the great events of the farming year, because there was not enough fodder to keep every animal alive through the winter. The meat had to be preserved at once, and a household that had run out of salt in November might go hungry by February. Families therefore counted their salt as carefully as they counted their grain, and a spoiled barrel was a real family disaster.

Because salted food did not spoil quickly, it could be carried on journeys that would otherwise have been impossible, and it made large armies and distant voyages practical. A commander planning a campaign had to count his men, his horses and his barrels of salt, and many a march failed through want of the last. In that sense salt gave a ruler a longer reach, and an army without it was only a crowd of hungry men.

Since no household could live without it, whoever controlled the salt controlled in some measure the food supply of everyone who depended on it. That gave salt a power that no spice or jewel could match, for a ruler could do without pepper but his people could not do without salt. It is no accident that so many of the great stories of salt turn out to be stories about power.

Wherever the climate was hot and dry, people learned to lead seawater into broad, shallow ponds and wait for the sun and the wind to do the work. As the water evaporated, the brine grew stronger, until a crust of white crystals formed on the bottom. It was the cheapest method of all, since the only fuel it needed was sunlight.

On the Atlantic coast of France, near Guérande, salt workers have farmed the same grey marshes for more than a thousand years. In summer they drag long wooden rakes across the clay ponds, gather the crystals into glittering heaps and carry them away in wheelbarrows. The work is slow and weather-dependent, and a single week of rain can undo a month of patient effort.

In cold and rainy countries the sun was too feeble to dry the brine, so the salt-makers had to boil it, using vast iron or lead pans set over roaring fires. The water vanished as steam, and the salt was raked out as a damp white heap and dried in baskets. It was hot, smoky and exhausting work, and the fires were rarely allowed to go out for long.

A busy salt works could consume an entire forest in a few decades, and in many places the price of fuel was greater than all the wages put together. Whole woodlands were felled to feed the fires, and when the trees were gone, the salt-makers had to buy wood from farther and farther away. The arrival of cheap coal eased the shortage of fuel, though only by creating new kinds of smoke and new kinds of trouble.

Where salt lay in thick buried beds, miners dug down to it and cut out great halls, leaving columns of solid salt to hold up the roof. The method is known as room-and-pillar mining, and it has been used for centuries because it is simple and dependable. A well-designed salt mine is a strangely beautiful place, with white walls glittering in the lamplight.

High in the Austrian Alps, beside a green lake, the mines of Hallstatt were worked for more than three thousand years. Miners sank shafts into the mountain and carried the heavy salt out on their backs, and the wealth it produced made the whole region famous. Even the name of the nearby city of Salzburg means Salt Castle, a reminder of what once paid its bills.

Salt, which preserves meat, preserves other things as well, and the Hallstatt tunnels have kept scraps of cloth, leather caps, wooden handles and even leftover food for thousands of years. Scientists have studied these remains and learned a great deal about the miners' clothing, their meals and their skills. The mountain, in effect, has been guarding a library of ordinary life, and its pages are still being read.

In the large cemetery beside the mine, archaeologists have found graves filled with bronze weapons, decorated pottery and ornaments made of materials that came from distant lands. Scholars generally conclude that the salt trade paid for these treasures, and they have named a whole period of European prehistory after the town. Few places in the world can claim that a mineral gave its name to a whole age of history.

Many modern salt companies no longer send miners underground at all, but drill a well into a salt bed and pump fresh water down through it. The water dissolves the mineral and is drawn back up as brine, which is then evaporated or sent straight to factories that need it. The method is safer than mining underground, though it can leave large hollows beneath the surface and must be watched with care.

In a modern vacuum pan, the brine boils inside a sealed vessel from which most of the air has been removed, and at that low pressure it turns to steam at a much lower temperature. This saves enormous amounts of fuel compared with the old open pans over blazing fires, and it produces fine, even crystals. It is a long way from a woman stirring a pot of brine, and yet the principle is the same.

In the basin of Sichuan, in western China, brine lies hidden deep beneath the hills, and the people who lived there began to drill for it more than two thousand years ago. These were among the first deep wells ever sunk anywhere in the world, and nothing like them existed in Europe for centuries. They were not dug with shovels but drilled with iron tools hung on bamboo ropes, a method that was remarkably clever.

Above the hole stood a tall wooden frame, and from it hung a heavy iron bit on a cable made of twisted bamboo. Workers jumped on a long wooden lever to lift the bit and let it fall, and each blow broke away a little more of the rock below. The progress was measured in a few finger-widths a day, so a deep well might take years.

As the shallow brine ran out, the well-diggers of Sichuan were forced to go deeper, and over the centuries their wells sank farther into the earth. One famous well, finished in 1835, is said to have reached a depth of about a thousand metres after more than ten years of work. For its time it was an astonishing achievement, and the men who built it left no names.

Raising the brine from such depths was heavy work, and the people of Sichuan solved it with the help of animals. Water buffalo walked in circles to turn a huge wooden drum, which wound up a long bamboo tube, and each time the tube reached the surface it let out a gush of brine. The whole system was built almost entirely from wood and bamboo, with very little metal, and it worked well for generations.

Sometimes a drill broke into a pocket of natural gas, which hissed out of the hole and could be set alight. The people of Sichuan learned to lead it through bamboo pipes to the furnaces and to burn it under their salt pans, saving great quantities of wood. It was an early example of a community turning a hazard into a resource.

Under the Han dynasty, about two thousand years ago, the imperial government decided that the profits from salt and iron should belong to the state rather than to private merchants. Officials set up workshops and offices across the empire, and only those with permission were allowed to produce or sell the goods. The money was badly needed, for the emperors were fighting expensive wars on their northern frontier.

In 81 BCE a great debate was held at the Han court, in which government officials defended the salt and iron monopoly against a group of scholars who attacked it. The officials argued that the revenue paid for the army and kept the frontier safe, while the scholars replied that high prices and poor tools were crushing the farmers. A record of the quarrel survives under the title Discourses on Salt and Iron, and it is still read today by students of Chinese history.

The logic that drew the Han emperors to salt drew many later rulers to it as well, for it was the perfect thing to tax. Every household had to buy it, whether rich or poor, and the supply came from a few known places where officials could count every sack. A tax on salt therefore raised money steadily, though it also fell most heavily on those with least.

Over the centuries, the revenue from salt in China helped to pay for armies, granaries, roads and the digging of canals. At some moments in history, in the Tang dynasty especially, it is said to have supplied as much as half of the government's income. A ruler who lost control of his salt works might find that he could no longer pay his soldiers at all.

Those merchants who held official licences to trade in salt could grow fabulously wealthy, since the state had made sure that nobody else could compete with them. In the city of Yangzhou, on the Grand Canal, such families built splendid gardens, collected paintings and gave generous patronage to scholars and artists. The city's elegance was paid for, one grain at a time, by the humble commodity on every table.

West of the Nile, in a valley called Wadi Natrun, shallow lakes dry up each summer and leave behind a crust of pale minerals. The Egyptians called this substance natron, and they gathered it by the cartload, for it was a mixture of ordinary salt with other salts that cleaned and dried. It was one of the most valuable gifts that the desert gave to the people who lived along the river.

When an Egyptian of rank died, the embalmers removed certain organs, covered the body in natron and left it for about forty days while the moisture drained away. The dried body was then washed, anointed with oils and resins and wrapped in many layers of linen. It was a long and costly process, and it explains why mummies have lasted for thousands of years.

The embalmers did not know about bacteria, but they had discovered the same principle that preserved a salted fish: where there is no moisture, decay cannot take hold. Salt and natron take the water out, and what is left can survive for ages, whether it is a fillet of perch or a pharaoh. The only real difference between the two was the dignity of the occasion, and the cost of the linen that was used afterward.

The river Nile teemed with fish, and in the season of plenty the Egyptians dried and salted the surplus so that it could be eaten later or sold to people far from the water. Waterbirds were treated in the same way, and both kinds of food appear in paintings of daily life on tomb walls. For the poor, salted fish was an everyday meal and a welcome change from bread.

Natron served the living as well as the dead, for its soapy qualities made it a good cleanser for skin, linen and dishes. Later craftsmen discovered that it helped sand melt at a lower temperature, and it became a key ingredient in the making of glass. Egypt was thus exporting a mineral that was needed in kitchens, temples and workshops alike.

Between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates, the farmers of ancient Mesopotamia fed their crops by irrigation, but the watering carried salts up through the soil until they formed a white crust at the surface. Some scholars think this slow poisoning of the land hurt the wheat harvests of the south and weakened its cities, though the question is still debated. It shows that salt, in the wrong place, can be as dangerous as it is useful.

The Dead Sea, between Israel and Jordan, is so intensely salty that it is many times saltier than any ocean, and no fish can survive in its water. Its Hebrew name means the Salt Sea, and the peoples of the region have taken salt, tar and healing mud from its shores for thousands of years. Visitors who wade in today still float on its surface as easily as a cork, and many of them come to read the newspaper there.

The Phoenicians, whose homeland lay on the coast of what is now Lebanon, built cities such as Tyre and Sidon and sailed boldly all over the Mediterranean. They traded in many goods, and it seems likely that salt and salted fish were among them, for the colonies they founded in Spain and North Africa later became famous for fish-salting. Their ships, in a sense, carried the first great network of salt across the Mediterranean, long before Rome grew strong.

Greek cities such as Athens were crowded and short of farmland, and they relied on ships to bring in food from distant shores. Among the imports were jars of salted fish from the Black Sea region, which fed ordinary citizens and were sold in markets and cookshops. Without salt, the Greeks could not have maintained such large towns on such small territories.

The poet Homer, who lived more than twenty-five centuries ago, called salt divine, and the phrase tells us how much the ancient Greeks respected it. In the ancient world it was used in religious ceremonies, and the Romans sprinkled a mixture of coarse flour and salt on animals offered to the gods as a sign of purity. The idea that salt was a sacred thing, rather than a mere seasoning, appears again and again in the cultures of the Mediterranean.

At the mouth of the river Tiber, about fifteen miles from Rome, the marshes held shallow pans where the sun dried seawater into salt. An old tradition says that the port of Ostia was first founded to protect these salt works, and the city that grew there later became the harbour of the whole empire. If the story is true, then salt helped to give Rome its gateway to the sea.

The Via Salaria, which means the Salt Road, was an ancient track that existed long before Rome grew into an empire. Traders from the Sabine hills used it to carry salt up from the coast, and later the Romans paved it and extended it across the mountains to the Adriatic Sea. Every traveller who walked along it, whatever his errand, was following in the footsteps of salt.

As the Roman state grew, it took a close interest in salt, and the historian Livy reports that the government controlled and fixed its price. In 204 BCE the official Marcus Livius put a tax on salt and was given the nickname Salinator, which means the Salt Man. Because the tax was unpopular with ordinary people, the name was probably not meant as a compliment at all.

Our word salary comes from the Latin salarium, and Roman writers such as Pliny connected it with sal, the word for salt. Some said that soldiers had once been paid in salt or given an allowance to buy it, but modern scholars are not sure, and the true story may be more complicated. Still, the very doubt shows how closely salt and money were linked in the Roman mind.

Salt left its mark on our language, for the Latin word sal lies behind many familiar English words. Salad originally meant something salted, such as leaves dressed with brine, while sauce and sausage both come from words for salted things, and salami follows the same pattern. Even a simple lunch of bread, sausage and salad can contain a small lesson in Roman vocabulary, if you know where to look.

Along the shores of Spain, North Africa and the Black Sea, the Romans built large fish-salting factories with stone tanks for packing the catch in salt. The products were loaded into clay jars and shipped to cities all around the empire, where hungry citizens bought them in markets and cookshops. It was one of the first food industries to operate on a truly international scale.

Garum, the favourite sauce of the Roman world, was made by layering small fish and fish parts with salt in large vats and leaving the mixture to ferment in the sun for weeks. The rich, savoury liquid was then drained, strained and bottled, and it added a salty depth of flavour to everything from soups to sweet dishes. Writers complained about the smell of the factories, but nobody seems to have complained about the taste.

The town of Pompeii, which was buried under ash when Vesuvius erupted in the year 79, was famous for its garum, and some of the best-known producers were based there. Archaeologists have uncovered shops, vats and storage jars, some of them painted with the names of the makers and even a mark of quality. The ash that destroyed the town also preserved this evidence of everyday trade, so we know more about its sauce than about many of its rulers.

The Roman statesman Cato, who wrote a handbook of advice for landowners, included a careful recipe for salting hams, with details on how much salt to use and how long to leave the meat. His instructions remind us that preserving food was a basic task on every farm, and that a farm without salt could not feed its household through the winter. Rome's greatness, in other words, rested on a great many humble tasks of this kind, performed quietly by people whose names we do not know.

After the Romans conquered Britain, they quickly discovered the salt springs of Droitwich and the Cheshire towns, and they set up works to boil the brine in lead pans. The salt was carried out along roads, and some old routes in the English countryside are still known as salt ways. The empire had arrived, and it had brought its appetite for salt along with its soldiers.

West Africa was divided by nature into regions that needed one another, since the humid lands of the south held gold and the burning Sahara to the north held salt. People who lived in the damp, hot south lost much salt through sweat and had little of it in their food, so they would gladly pay a high price. This difference between the two regions created a trade that was to last for the better part of a thousand years.

Camels were brought to North Africa about two thousand years ago, and these patient animals made the crossing of the Sahara possible. They could go for days without water and carry heavy loads, so merchants organised caravans of hundreds of animals that carried salt southward and returned laden with gold and ivory. Without the camel, the great trade of the Sahara could hardly have begun, and the map of West Africa might look quite different.

In 1352 the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta arrived at Taghaza, a settlement in the middle of the Sahara, and described what he saw with evident astonishment. The houses and even the mosque were built of slabs of salt and roofed with camel skins, because there were no trees in the whole place. He thought it a remarkable town, though not at all a pleasant one, and he was glad to leave it behind him.

Ibn Battuta did not enjoy his stay at Taghaza, and he said so in his account. The water was brackish, the place was hot and bleak, and the workers had nothing to eat except what the caravans brought them from far away. Their whole lives revolved around salt, which they dug from pits and traded for food, and nothing else gave the town a reason to exist.

The salt was cut from the ground into large slabs, and each camel carried two of them, one on either side of its body. A loaded caravan then set out across the sand for the southern markets, and the crossing took weeks of burning days and bitterly cold nights. A single mistake at a well could mean the end of the entire expedition.

By the sixteenth century the workings at Taghaza were running down, and a new mining centre at Taoudenni, farther south, took over the trade. Even now, a few caravans of camels still make the long journey carrying salt slabs across the desert to the towns of the south. The tradition is fading as lorries replace camels on the sand, but it has not yet disappeared from the desert.

The city of Timbuktu stood at the edge of the desert, at a point where the caravan routes met the river, and it grew into the main market for the trade between the Sahara and the south. Merchants came from many countries, and with the money they left behind the city founded schools and libraries that became famous across the Muslim world. The wealth that built them began, at least in part, with the slabs of salt that arrived on the backs of camels.

There is a famous saying that, in the markets of the Sahel, salt was once worth its weight in gold. Historians doubt that the exchange was ever as simple or as regular as that, but there is no doubt that both goods were precious and that rulers, such as the kings of Mali, taxed both of them. The story survives, in all its forms, because it feels true to the spirit of the trade even if it is not true to the letter.

In the highlands of Ethiopia, shaped bars of salt known as amole were used as small change for centuries, and they were still accepted in some markets during the twentieth century. A buyer would pay with a bar, and a seller who needed smaller change could simply break one in half. Even the thinnest slice remained exactly as useful as the day it was cut, and a broken bar lost none of its worth.

In the Danakil Depression, a low and blistering plain in the north of Ethiopia, workers of the Afar people still cut blocks of salt by hand, as their ancestors did. Temperatures can rise above forty degrees, yet the workers rise before dawn, chop the crust into slabs and trim them with axes, and load them onto camels for the long walk to the highlands. It is among the last places on Earth where this ancient and exhausting trade still survives in its old form.

The Maya of Central America made salt on the coasts of Mexico and Belize, where archaeologists have found the remains of wooden workshops and thousands of broken boiling pots. Workers boiled seawater in the pots over wood fires, and the salt was then carried inland by canoe and on human backs. Cities far from the sea, deep in the forest, depended on this steady supply.

The Aztecs lived in a valley with shallow, salty lakes, and they gathered the crystals from the shores and boiled the brine in pots. Salt was sold in the great market of their capital, Tenochtitlan, and the people honoured a goddess of salt, Huixtocihuatl, in their festivals. The Spanish who arrived in the sixteenth century were amazed by the order and variety of the trade.

High in the Peruvian Andes, above a river valley near Maras, a salty spring runs out of the mountain and feeds hundreds of small terraced pools. Families guide the water into the pools, wait for the sun to dry it and then scrape out the white crystals, exactly as people did long before the Inca. Each family owns its pools, and the skills are passed from parent to child.

In North America, long before European settlers arrived, many nations gathered salt from springs, licks and dry lakes and traded it with their neighbours. Some springs were used for generations, and the trails to them became roads of trade that settlers later followed. The famous springs of what is now central New York, where the Onondaga people lived, were among them, and we shall return to them later.

On the high plateau of Tibet, where almost nothing grows but grass, salt lakes provided a valuable commodity that the herders carried to the lower valleys on the backs of yaks. There they exchanged it for barley, which the farmers could grow and the herders could not, and the two groups depended on each other. Salt still gives its taste to the butter tea that Tibetans drink every day.

Japan has almost no rock salt and few salt lakes, so its people had to take their salt from the sea, and they developed some ingenious methods for doing so. Workers spread seawater on sandy beaches or on seaweed, collected the salty residue and then boiled the strong brine until the crystals formed. It was a slow process that demanded skill and a great deal of firewood.

In Russia, Poland and many neighbouring countries, an honoured guest may be welcomed at the door with a round loaf of bread and a small dish of salt, offered on a decorated cloth. The guest is expected to break off a piece, dip it in the salt and eat it, and the gesture means that he is received as a friend. It shows that salt, once so precious, still stands for hospitality, and that old customs can outlive the reasons that created them.

In a number of cultures, from the Middle East to South Asia, the person who has shared another's bread and salt is considered bound to him by loyalty. The Urdu and Hindi phrase namak halal, meaning true to the salt, describes a faithful friend, while its opposite is used for a betrayer. Such sayings show how deeply the shared meal and its salt were woven into the idea of trust.

In the Hebrew Bible, a covenant of salt means a promise that is lasting and cannot be broken, since salt does not decay. The Gospel of Matthew uses a different image when it describes the followers of Jesus as the salt of the earth, a phrase that has become common even among those who never read it. Both texts, in their different ways, treat salt as a symbol of something steady, valuable and good, which people can rely on.

In the Shinto tradition of Japan, salt is a symbol of purity that can drive away bad luck, and its use is woven into everyday life. Before a match, sumo wrestlers throw a handful of salt into the ring to cleanse it, and some restaurants place small cones of salt at their doors to welcome good fortune. These customs show that the human respect for salt has lasted far longer than the scarcity that created it.

The town of Lüneburg, in northern Germany, stands on a hill of salt, and its brine springs were already in use more than a thousand years ago. Its salt works boiled the brine in great lead pans, and the profits from the trade made the town one of the wealthiest in the region. The handsome brick houses that still stand there were paid for, in large part, with salt.

Behind the wealth of Lüneburg lay a heavy demand for fuel, and the forests of the surrounding countryside were cut down to feed the salt pans. The works also employed hundreds of labourers to stoke the fires, rake out the salt and load it into barrels, and the town's council guarded the business with great jealousy. Salt made the citizens rich, but it also made the surrounding countryside bare, and the loss was felt for generations.

From Lüneburg, a long track known as the Old Salt Road led northeast across forests and heath to Lübeck, a port on the Baltic Sea about a hundred kilometres away. Heavy carts loaded with salt barrels rolled along it in all weathers, and the inns, markets and toll posts along its edge grew into settlements of their own. It was one of the busiest trade routes of medieval Europe, and its name is still remembered by the people who live along it.

In the autumn, enormous shoals of herring gathered in the waters off southern Sweden, and the fishermen pulled in more than anyone could eat on the day. There was only one way to save the catch, and that was to pack the fish in salt, so merchants from Lübeck brought barrels of Lüneburg salt to the fairs by the shore. The partnership of salt and herring made fortunes for the merchants who understood it, and it fed millions of people at the same time.

Each herring had to be gutted within hours of being caught, and then it was packed in a barrel between thick layers of salt, with the top sealed tightly. The barrels were shipped across the Baltic and North Seas and carried inland by cart, and they fed towns, monasteries and armies far from any shore. Herring became the cheap and reliable protein of medieval Europe, and all of it depended on a steady supply of salt.

From the thirteenth century, the merchants of Lübeck and other northern towns joined together in an alliance that later became known as the Hanseatic League. The members shared the cost of protecting ships and agreed to support each other's trade, and they grew rich from salt, salted herring, grain, timber and furs. At its height, the League was a commercial power that kings had to treat with respect.

On the sunny Atlantic coast of France, in the Bay of Bourgneuf, salt could be made by evaporation for far less money than it cost to boil it over fires in Germany. Known as bay salt, it was carried north in Dutch ships and gradually took a large share of the market from Lüneburg. A change in the way salt was made had changed the balance of trade.

In the Netherlands, fishermen discovered that herring could be gutted and salted on board their boats, so the catch reached the port in fine condition. A legend gives the credit to a man named Willem Beukelszoon, though scholars are unsure whether he ever existed. Whatever its origin, the technique made the Dutch the leading herring merchants of Europe for centuries.

The republic of Venice built its power partly on salt, which it produced in the shallow lagoon around the city and also bought from other regions of the Mediterranean. It then sold the salt to the towns of northern Italy, sometimes making them agree to buy only from Venice, and the profits and taxes provided steady income. Few cities in history have turned seawater into palaces quite so thoroughly, or quite so profitably, as Venice did.

Venice managed its salt trade with a specialised government office, and it enforced the rules about who could buy and sell with great strictness. When rivals threatened its position, it was ready to fight, and in the 1480s a war with the neighbouring state of Ferrara was partly the result of rival salt works. The republic never forgot that part of its wealth had begun in the mud of the lagoon.

Beneath the town of Wieliczka, near the Polish city of Krakow, lies one of the oldest and greatest salt mines in the world. Miners began to work it in the thirteenth century and kept digging for roughly seven hundred years, creating a vast maze of tunnels, chambers and shafts. It is one of the few industrial sites that has become a place of pilgrimage for tourists.

The mines at Wieliczka and the neighbouring town of Bochnia were royal property, and the Polish crown drew a large part of its revenue from them for centuries. Salt money helped to pay for the court, to build castles and to support the kingdom's armies, and the miners enjoyed special privileges in return for their dangerous work. Poland's golden age, with its fine buildings and its famous university, rested in some measure on the salt beneath Krakow.

In time the mine at Wieliczka reached a depth of about three hundred metres, with miles of tunnels spread across nine levels. Miners descended by rope and ladder, and horses were lowered into the dark to pull carts loaded with salt, sometimes spending most of their working lives there. The mine was a dangerous place, with constant risks of collapse, flooding and fire, and the workers often prayed before they went down.

Over the centuries the miners of Wieliczka turned their workplace into a gallery of devotion, carving chapels, altars, statues and even whole scenes from the grey rock. The largest of these is the Chapel of Saint Kinga, which has salt chandeliers, reliefs and floors made entirely of the mineral. Their art, made in a dark and dangerous place, expressed hope and faith, and today it is visited by many thousands of people each year.

According to legend, a Hungarian princess named Kinga, who was about to marry a Polish prince, dropped her ring into a salt mine in her homeland and asked that salt might be found in her new country. When the miners of Wieliczka opened a lump of salt, they found a ring inside it. Historians cannot confirm the tale, but the people of the region love to tell it.

Salzburg, which means Salt Castle, took its name from the barges that carried salt along the river Salzach from the mines at Hallein, and the city became prosperous on the proceeds. Its rulers, who were archbishops as well as princes, used the money to build palaces, churches and fountains that still make the city beautiful. Few of the tourists who visit the birthplace of Mozart realise that the town itself was founded on salt.

In the early seventeenth century the Archbishop of Salzburg, Wolf Dietrich, quarrelled with neighbouring Bavaria over the salt trade, which both of them wished to control. In 1611 Bavarian soldiers marched into the city, and the archbishop, who had fled, was captured and imprisoned, remaining a captive until his death. The conflict is remembered as the Salt War, and it is a good example of how a quarrel over trade could bring down a prince.

The Domesday Book, compiled in 1086 on the orders of William the Conqueror, lists the salt houses of the Cheshire towns of Nantwich, Northwich and Middlewich. The ending wich in their names comes from an old word that came to mean a place where salt was made, and in many parts of England it still shows where salt was once worked. Place names, like layers of rock, can reveal the history of a landscape to anyone who knows how to read them.

In the wich towns of Cheshire, workers boiled the local brine in broad pans heated over fires in smoky wooden sheds, and then raked out the salt and dried it in baskets. Packhorses and carts carried it to markets across the Midlands and beyond, and some of the old routes can still be traced on the map. The trade was slow, hot and smelly, but for the people who controlled it, it paid very well indeed.

In 1670, a party searching for coal near Northwich struck a thick bed of rock salt instead, and the discovery transformed the industry of the whole county. The river Weaver was later made navigable, in the early eighteenth century, so that barges could carry the salt down to the port of Liverpool for shipment overseas. England had found a new source of wealth beneath its feet, and its merchants did not intend to waste it.

In the fourteenth century the kings of France, who were short of money for their wars, began to tax salt, and the levy became known as the gabelle. It proved so productive that it was kept and increased for four hundred years, becoming one of the most hated taxes in the kingdom. The French crown had found a source of money that its subjects could not avoid.

The gabelle was fiercely unequal, because the kingdom was divided into regions with very different rules. In the heartland around Paris salt was heavily taxed and expensive, in some provinces it was taxed lightly, and in a few, such as Brittany, it was free of tax altogether. A family's salt bill thus depended on which side of an invisible line it happened to live.

In the regions where the tax was heaviest, each household was forced to buy a fixed quantity of salt from the royal stores every year, regardless of how much it needed. The families had to pay the full price, and they were forbidden to resell what they did not use, so even a thrifty household could not escape the burden. Many people felt that the rule was less a tax than a form of theft.

The crown did not collect the gabelle itself but sold the right to private contractors known as tax farmers, who paid a fixed sum and kept whatever they could squeeze out of the taxpayers. Their guards, who were widely hated, had the right to stop travellers and to search carts and even private houses for salt on which the tax had not been paid. The system invited abuse, and the complaints of ordinary people show that abuses were frequent, cruel and rarely punished.

The difference in prices was an irresistible temptation, for salt that cost a few coins in Brittany could be sold for many times as much in the heart of France. Smugglers, known as false salt-sellers, bought it cheaply and crept across the boundary at night, dodging patrols and avoiding roads. Some were poor families looking for bread, while others were organised gangs that earned a great deal of money.

The penalties for smuggling a sack of salt across the boundary were harsh, and they were not applied lightly or mercifully. A convicted smuggler could be fined heavily, imprisoned or condemned to the galleys, where he would row the king's warships in chains, and those who were caught armed or in a gang might even be put to death. Over the years, many thousands of men, women and children were punished for the crime of carrying a sack of salt.

When the French Revolution began in 1789, people across the country sent lists of grievances to the capital, and the gabelle was among the most frequent complaints. The new national assembly agreed that it was unjust and cruel, and in 1790 it abolished the tax altogether, to the great joy of the villagers. The prisoners who had been condemned for smuggling salt were released from their chains.

The memory of the gabelle did not stop later rulers from noticing how easy salt was to tax, and in 1806 the emperor Napoleon introduced a new levy on it to pay for his wars. In a milder form, the tax survived through the nineteenth century and was finally abolished in 1945. Governments, it seems, find it very hard to resist something that everybody has to buy.

In 1646 the Russian government, guided by the powerful minister Boris Morozov, put a heavy tax on salt, and the price rose sharply across the country. Many families could not afford the salt they needed to preserve their fish, and the catch rotted on the riverbanks while the treasury collected less than expected. The tax was withdrawn in 1647, but the anger that it had caused did not go away with it.

In 1648 an angry crowd marched through Moscow to petition the young tsar Alexis, and when officials tried to disperse it, the protest turned into a riot that is remembered as the Salt Riot. The mob attacked the houses of unpopular officials, including that of Boris Morozov, and the tsar, fearing for his throne, sent his minister out of the city. Historians add that other taxes and corrupt officials also fed the fury, but the name has stuck.

A ship setting out on a voyage of many months could not carry fresh meat, since it would rot within days, and so its barrels were filled with beef and pork preserved in brine. The salted meat was stacked in the hold with biscuits, dried peas and casks of water, and these simple supplies made the great voyages of discovery possible. In a very real sense, the age of exploration sailed on salt, and every great captain depended on the humble barrel.

Sailors in the English navy had a joking name for their salted beef, which they called salt horse, and they complained that it was tough as leather and almost as old. The cook had to soak it for hours in fresh water before it could be eaten, and even then it was a plain and chewy meal. Still, it kept for months at a time, and a hungry sailor on a long voyage would eat it gladly and be grateful for it.

The explorers of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, such as Christopher Columbus and Ferdinand Magellan, carried salted meat and fish among the supplies on which their crews depended. Without them, journeys of many months across unknown seas would have been impossible, however brave the captains might be. Every voyage required the support of a long chain of salt works, barrel makers and merchants on land.

Salted meat and hard biscuit were safe from rot, but they contained almost no vitamin C, and on long voyages thousands of sailors died of scurvy, a disease that causes weakness, bleeding gums and slow-healing wounds. The cure, fresh citrus fruit, was tested by the naval doctor James Lind in 1747 but was not generally adopted for many more years. Salt had enabled the voyages, but by itself it could not keep the sailors healthy, and the lesson was learned at a terrible cost.

The Basques, who lived on both sides of the Pyrenees by the Bay of Biscay, were among the boldest fishermen of medieval Europe, and they pursued cod and whales far out into the Atlantic. Some historians believe that Basque boats reached the waters off Newfoundland even before Columbus sailed, but the evidence is slight, and the question remains disputed. What is certain is that cod became the great prize of the Atlantic, and that salt was needed to turn it into a commodity.

In the waters off Newfoundland, fishermen used two principal methods of preparing their cod. They could pack it in salt in the hold of the ship, producing what was called green cod, or they could split it, salt it and dry it on wooden racks on the shore. The dried version was as hard as a board and would keep for years, and in both cases the work of preserving was done by salt.

In Catholic Europe the Church forbade meat on Fridays and throughout Lent, and the demand for fish was therefore enormous, which suited the merchants who sold salted cod. It sold well in Spain, Portugal and Italy, and the dish called bacalao or bacalhau is still a favourite in those countries, with hundreds of recipes. The religious calendar had created a regular appetite for fish, and salt was the only means of satisfying it at a reasonable price.

The poorest grade of salt cod, known as West India cod, was sent in large quantities to the islands of the Caribbean, where it was used to feed the enslaved Africans who worked on the sugar plantations. It was part of a trading system built on forced labour, in which food, sugar, salt and human beings were all treated as goods. This dark connection is a reminder that salt has a moral history as well.

From the late 1600s, sailors from Bermuda began to visit the Turks Islands in the Caribbean, where the sun dried seawater in natural ponds and left a rich crop of salt. They raked it into heaps and loaded it onto ships bound for the colonies of North America, where it was needed for the fisheries and for the preservation of meat. The islands seemed to produce wealth almost without effort, though the effort was in fact being made by others.

The hard labour on the Turks Islands was done mainly by enslaved Africans, who raked the salt for hours under a blazing sun and waded through brine that burned their skin and caused painful sores. Their owners grew rich, while the workers had little protection, and their slavery ended only when it was abolished in the British Empire in 1834. Their suffering is part of the story of salt, and it should not be forgotten.

Before the American Revolution, most of the salt used in the colonies had been imported from Europe and the West Indies. When the war began in 1775, British warships blockaded the harbours, and the shortage of salt became a serious worry for the army, which could not keep its meat from spoiling. Without salt, it was hard for an army to eat, and it was even harder for the general to keep his soldiers loyal.

Along the coasts of New England and the middle colonies, ordinary people began to make salt by boiling seawater in kettles and evaporating it in shallow pans. Several state governments encouraged the effort by offering rewards to anyone who started a salt works, since the war could not be won with hungry soldiers. The results were modest at first, but they showed what necessity could achieve when a young country was determined to be free.

In what is now central New York, the Onondaga people, members of the Haudenosaunee confederacy, had used the salty springs beside their lake for many generations before the arrival of Europeans. In 1654 a French priest named Simon Le Moyne tasted the water and wrote one of the first European accounts of the springs. He thought it excellent, and so would many Americans after him, though by then the Onondaga had lost much of their land.

In the years after the Revolution, settlers arrived at the lake, boiled the brine in rows of iron kettles and sold the salt to farmers and traders across the region. The State of New York took control of the springs and charged a small duty on every barrel, a revenue that proved remarkably useful in the years ahead. Salt, once again, was becoming an instrument of government as well as a gift of nature, and its profits were beginning to build a state.

The Erie Canal, completed in 1825, was a ditch of about three hundred and sixty miles that joined the Hudson River to Lake Erie and opened the interior of North America to trade. It passed close to the salt works of Syracuse, and barges loaded with barrels could now travel cheaply to distant markets, while the duty on salt helped to repay the cost of the canal. Few cargoes suited the new waterway better than salt, which was heavy, cheap and needed in every settlement along the route.

The town of Syracuse prospered so quickly that it became known as the Salt City, and its streets were lined with salt works, barrel makers and warehouses. Some of the brine was boiled, but a good deal was dried in the sun in long wooden vats that had movable roofs, which could be rolled across to protect the contents when it rained. The industry employed thousands of people at its height, and the work of those people built the city that we see there today.

From the canal ports the salt went on west, by lake steamers and river boats, to the farms and the towns of the new settlements. In cities such as Cincinnati, which earned the nickname of Porkopolis, meat packers needed vast quantities of salt to cure the pork they shipped across the country and abroad. The westward growth of the nation was fuelled by salted meat as much as by anything else.

When the Civil War began in 1861, the South depended on imports of salt from abroad, and the Union navy's blockade of its ports soon cut off the supply. The price rose to many times its former level, and the shortage threatened the armies as well as the civilians, since salt was needed for preserving meat, curing leather and keeping horses healthy. Some people dug up the earth floors of their smokehouses to boil out the salt that had dripped into the soil.

The most important source of Confederate salt was Saltville, in the mountains of Virginia, where hundreds of kettles were kept boiling day and night. The Union tried to capture it in October 1864 and was beaten back, but a second raid in December succeeded, and the works were badly damaged. In the same war, a newly discovered salt dome at Avery Island in Louisiana also supplied the South until Union troops overran it.

The shortage of salt, though only one of many problems, damaged the South's ability to feed its soldiers and its families, and it contributed to hunger and discontent in the final years of the war. It showed once more what rulers had known for thousands of years: that an army marches on its stomach, and that its stomach depends on something as simple as salt. Nobody who lived through those years was likely to forget that lesson, and the generals of later wars remembered it too.

As the eighteenth century advanced, the new industries of Europe needed ever larger amounts of soda ash, which was used in making glass, soap, paper and textiles. It had traditionally come from the ashes of burnt seaweed and certain coastal plants, and these sources were too limited to satisfy the growing demand. A cheaper and more abundant supply was urgently needed, and the governments of Europe were prepared to reward anyone who could provide it.

In 1783 the French Academy of Sciences, aware that the country depended on imported soda, offered a prize to anyone who could devise a way of making it from common salt. The idea was attractive because salt was cheap and abundant, whereas the natural sources of soda were few and costly. The challenge attracted many inventors, though few of them had any real idea how to succeed.

Nicolas Leblanc, a French doctor and chemist, took up the challenge and patented a method in 1791. First he treated salt with sulphuric acid, then he heated the result with limestone and coal, and out came soda ash, the substance that industry desired. The process was complicated and dirty, but it worked, and it would transform the chemical trade.

Sadly, Leblanc himself never reaped the reward of his idea, for the turmoil of the Revolution led to the seizure of his factory and the publication of his secrets. He never received the prize that had been promised, and he died in poverty in 1806, while others grew rich using his method. His story is a reminder that justice and genius do not always go together.

In the nineteenth century, the Leblanc process was taken up with enthusiasm in northern England, where factories at Liverpool, St Helens and Widnes were built to use the Cheshire salt. They produced soda ash in enormous quantities, and the product was sold across the world to glassmakers, soap boilers and cloth manufacturers. The region became one of the great chemical centres of the age, though it paid a heavy price.

The Leblanc process had an ugly secret, for it released clouds of hydrochloric acid gas that drifted from the tall chimneys over the neighbouring fields. Crops withered, trees died and the washing hung out to dry was ruined, while the local people complained that the gas harmed their lungs. For many years the manufacturers argued that smoke was simply the smell of prosperity.

In 1863 the British Parliament passed the Alkali Act, which required the soda makers to capture nearly all of the hydrochloric acid gas that escaped from their works. It was one of the first laws of its kind, and it created a body of inspectors to check that the rules were followed. The act showed that the state could, if it wished, protect the public from the cost of industry.

In the 1860s, the Belgian chemist Ernest Solvay perfected a process that used ammonia as a go-between, so that salt, limestone and carbon dioxide could be turned into soda ash with far less waste. The new method was cleaner and cheaper than Leblanc's, and over the following decades it drove the older process out of business. Chemistry, like trade, tends to reward the person who finds the better way, and Solvay's name is still on the factories.

Two English partners, John Brunner and Ludwig Mond, built a large factory at Northwich, in the heart of Cheshire's salt country, in the 1870s, and used the Solvay process there. The local brine and the limestone of the nearby hills provided the raw materials, and the works grew into one of the most important chemical companies in Britain. Cheshire's salt, which had been boiled in pans since Roman times, had found its modern master and its modern purpose.

Later still, engineers learned that an electric current passed through brine splits it into hydrogen, chlorine and a strong alkali known as caustic soda, and this process is now one of the most important in the chemical industry. The products are used to make bleach, paper, plastics and cleaning agents, and chlorine helps to make drinking water safe in cities around the world. Even today, a great deal of the salt that is mined never reaches a dinner table, but goes instead into factories like these.

The people of India had been making salt for thousands of years along their long coasts, in their dry salt lakes and from their salt-bearing earth, and earlier rulers had taxed it too. In the late eighteenth century, however, the East India Company, a British trading firm that had become a ruling power, took control of the salt trade in Bengal. The Company's chief aim was revenue, and salt, which every household had to buy, was an obvious target.

Under British rule, salt carried a heavy duty, and the government kept a close watch over who was allowed to produce or sell it. Indian families who lived beside the sea were forbidden to collect salt for themselves, and anyone who made it without permission could be fined or sent to prison. The law, in effect, treated a gift of nature as the property of the state, and the state meant to be paid for it.

For many years British merchants shipped salt from Cheshire to Bengal, sometimes using it as ballast for ships that would return with Indian goods. Heavy taxes on local salt made imports cheaper than the product of Indian workers, who lost much of their trade, and the whole system seemed designed to benefit the rulers rather than the ruled. Indians noticed this unfairness at the time, and they remembered it for generations, long after the ships had stopped sailing.

To stop salt from crossing the boundaries between taxed and untaxed regions, the British built an inland customs line that eventually stretched for more than two thousand miles across India. Much of it was a living barrier of thorny bushes and trees, planted so densely that neither man nor animal could easily pass, and guarded by thousands of officers. It became known as the Great Hedge of India, and for decades it formed one of the longest barriers ever grown by human hands.

Guards patrolled the hedge day and night, and anyone who wanted to cross it had to pass through a gate, where officers searched baggage and carts for untaxed salt. A traveller found with salt that had not been taxed could be fined or imprisoned, and a family with a small business could be ruined. The hedge was a very long wall, built to protect what was, in the end, a tax on a pinch of salt.

By about 1879 the British had brought the different salt duties of their Indian territories closer together, and the customs line was therefore no longer needed. The hedge was left to rot, and it soon disappeared from the landscape and from memory, but the tax that it had guarded remained in place. It would last for nearly seven more decades, long enough to become the cause of a famous march.

The salt tax was a flat charge on each unit of salt, which meant that it took the same amount from every family, no matter how much money they had. A labourer who earned very little therefore paid a far larger share of his income than a rich merchant did, and the extra cost fell hardest on those who sweated the most. For this reason, critics in India and Britain alike called the tax unfair, and they said that it punished people for being poor.

Indian leaders had objected to the salt tax for decades, and in meetings and newspapers they described it as an unjust burden on the poor. The Indian National Congress, which was founded in 1885 and gradually grew into a mass movement, demanded a voice for Indians in their own government and later demanded independence altogether. The salt tax was only one of its many grievances, but it was a grievance that every Indian could understand, because every Indian ate salt.

In January 1930 the Indian National Congress declared that the goal of its movement was complete independence from British rule, and it asked Mohandas Gandhi to lead a campaign of civil disobedience. Many ideas were suggested about how to begin, and Gandhi spent weeks considering the matter. Everybody wondered what he would choose, and few of them guessed that the answer would be a pinch of salt.

Gandhi chose salt because every person needed it, because the tax hurt the poorest most and because the law could be broken peacefully by anyone who picked up a handful from the shore. Some of his colleagues were puzzled by the choice, and even sceptical, but his judgement of what ordinary people could understand proved to be remarkably sound. Time would show that his judgement had been right, for the simple act that he proposed would be understood in every village.

On 2 March 1930 Gandhi wrote a long letter to the Viceroy of India, Lord Irwin, in which he described the salt tax as a cruel burden on the poor and announced that he would break the salt law. He sent it by the hand of a young English admirer, and the answer that came back expressed regret in cold and formal words. The viceroy did not seem to understand what was coming, and neither, perhaps, did many of Gandhi's own friends.

At Sabarmati, near the city of Ahmedabad, Gandhi lived in a simple community, called an ashram, with a number of followers who shared his way of life. For the march he chose seventy-eight of them, who came from many parts of India and who included both young students and older men. They were not soldiers, and they carried no weapons, only bundles of clothes and a few belongings.

At dawn on 12 March 1930, after the morning prayers, Gandhi, who was sixty years old, set out with his companions from the gates of the ashram and walked toward the sea. A great crowd had gathered to see him go, and thousands of people lined the road to watch the thin figure with his walking stick stride off into the haze. The journey that he had promised, and that the whole country had been waiting for, was beginning at last.

The marchers set out each morning before the heat of the day and walked about ten miles through the villages of Gujarat, resting at midday and again at evening. The whole journey measured some two hundred and forty miles, nearly four hundred kilometres, and it took twenty-four days to complete. Gandhi kept a regular schedule, and the discipline of the walk was part of its message.

In every village that they passed, crowds came out to welcome the walkers, sprinkling the dusty road with water, scattering leaves and flowers and bringing food and drink. In the evenings Gandhi spoke to the villagers about the salt tax, about the need to remain peaceful and about their duty to refuse to obey an unjust law. Many who came to look at the famous man stayed to listen to what he had to say, and went home as supporters of his cause.

As the march passed through the countryside, a number of village officials, who were paid by the government, resigned their positions in order to support it, and the loss of local administrators troubled the British. Meanwhile, more and more volunteers joined the line of walkers, so that the group grew from seventy-eight to many hundreds before it reached the sea. The movement was gathering strength with every mile, and the walk was no longer a small demonstration but a national event.

Journalists from India and abroad followed the walkers, and newspapers in many countries ran daily reports of their progress. Readers in London and New York learned of the elderly man in a loincloth who was marching across the plains to protest against a tax on salt, and many of them found the picture hard to forget. The march had become a story that no government, however powerful, could entirely control, and the pictures travelled faster than the walkers.

British officials were uncertain how to respond to the march, and some of them dismissed the plan as foolish, doubting that a handful of salt could threaten an empire. The viceroy hesitated to arrest Gandhi, fearing that to jail him would only make the old man more famous and the movement stronger. In the end, the government chose to wait and see what would happen, and so the walkers simply walked on toward the sea.

On 5 April 1930, after twenty-four days of walking, the marchers arrived at Dandi, a small village beside the Arabian Sea, where crowds of supporters and journalists were waiting. The walkers were tired and dusty, but they were in good spirits, and that evening they held a prayer meeting beside the water. Few people slept much that night, for everyone knew what the morning would bring.

On the morning of 6 April 1930, Gandhi bathed in the sea and then walked up the beach to a place where the tide had left a crust of salty mud. He stooped, picked up a small lump of natural salt, and held it in his hand for the crowd to see, and in doing so he broke the British law that forbade Indians to make salt. The movement had begun, and a small handful of salt in an old man's hand had become a symbol that the whole country understood.

After the events at Dandi, people all over India began to make their own salt in defiance of the law, boiling seawater in pans on the beaches and scraping the white crust from the shore. In cities such as Bombay and Calcutta, small packets of illegal salt were sold openly, and a pinch of it became a prized souvenir. A law that very large numbers of people no longer respected could not easily be enforced, however many policemen were sent out.

The authorities responded with arrests, and over the following months tens of thousands of people were jailed for making or selling salt, or for joining the protests. Women took part in unprecedented numbers, marching, picketing shops and facing the police, and the prisons were soon overflowing with peaceful lawbreakers. It was becoming clear that force alone would not end the movement, and that the jails could not hold everybody who wished to join it.

In the early hours of 5 May 1930, a few weeks after the salt had been lifted at Dandi, police arrived at the camp where Gandhi was sleeping and took him into custody. He was held without trial at Yerwada prison, near the city of Pune, and the protests did not stop, for his followers had been prepared for the moment. The movement no longer depended on a single man, and the leaders who took his place were prepared to go on in the same peaceful way.

On 21 May 1930, the poet and political leader Sarojini Naidu led a column of about two and a half thousand volunteers toward the Dharasana Salt Works, a government factory on the coast of Gujarat. They intended to walk in and take the salt, using no violence whatever, and they had been trained to accept whatever happened to them without raising a hand. It was one of the most disciplined acts of protest of the whole century, and it was about to be tested to the limit.

At the gates of the works, police armed with long steel-tipped batons struck the volunteers as they walked forward in lines, and the marchers fell without lifting a hand in defence. As soon as one wave was beaten down, another came up behind it, and the rows kept advancing in silence through the dust. Those who watched found the sight hard to forget, and many of them were moved by the calm courage of the marchers.

An American journalist named Webb Miller was present at Dharasana, and he described what he saw in a detailed report that was telegraphed around the world, despite efforts to censor it. Newspapers in the United States and Britain printed it in full, and readers learned that the police were beating peaceful protesters who did not defend themselves. Public opinion in many countries began to turn against the methods used to defend British rule in India, and the government in London felt the change.

The reports from Dharasana embarrassed the British government, which could not claim to be ruling with the consent of the governed while its police were beating peaceful volunteers in front of foreign reporters. By January 1931 the viceroy had decided that negotiation was wiser than repression, and he released Gandhi and invited him to talk. It was a remarkable change of position for a government that had once been inclined to dismiss the march as trivial.

In March 1931 Gandhi and the viceroy, Lord Irwin, signed an agreement, known as the Gandhi–Irwin Pact, under which most of the political prisoners were released and the campaign was suspended. People living near the coast were allowed to make salt for their own use, though the tax itself remained in force for everyone else. It was a limited result, but it was widely seen as the first time that the British had negotiated with Gandhi as an equal.

Independence did not follow immediately, and the years after the salt campaign brought new campaigns, new imprisonments and long negotiations, while the Second World War placed enormous strains on Britain and its empire. Gandhi, Naidu and many thousands of others went back to prison during the struggle, and the movement grew in size and in confidence. The salt march was only the beginning of the final chapter, but it had shown the way and given the movement its confidence.

On 15 August 1947, India became an independent nation, and the salt tax that had provoked so much anger was soon swept away, closing a chapter that had lasted for the better part of two centuries. The march to the sea is remembered as one of the great moments of non-violent protest, and its example later inspired people in other lands who were struggling for their rights. A handful of salt, lifted from a beach by a man who refused to use force, had helped to change the course of history.

In the early nineteenth century a French confectioner named Nicolas Appert discovered that food sealed in glass jars and heated in boiling water would keep for months without spoiling. Within a few years the idea had been applied to tin cans, which were sturdy enough for armies and ships, and a new way of preserving food had appeared that did not depend on salt. It was the first small crack in the old order, though nobody at the time realised how far the crack would spread.

From the 1870s, engineers built machines that could make cold air, and soon railway wagons and steamships were fitted with refrigerated chambers that could carry fresh meat over thousands of miles. In 1882 the sailing ship Dunedin brought a cargo of frozen meat from New Zealand to Britain, and the voyage proved that distance no longer meant decay. Salt could no longer claim that it alone could feed the growing cities, and the great salt-fish and salt-pork trades began to shrink.

In the twentieth century the refrigerator moved from the factory and the butcher's shop into the ordinary kitchen, and families in rich countries could now keep milk, meat and vegetables fresh for days at a time.
