Salted food ceased to be a necessity for most people, and the autumn slaughter, with its barrels and crocks, became a memory of the older generation. The cold had done what no law or army had ever managed to do, and it had done it quietly, in ordinary kitchens.

Salted foods did not vanish when the need for them faded, because people had grown to love the flavours that salt and time can produce. Ham, bacon, hard cheese, anchovies and pickled vegetables remain popular in kitchens around the world, and today they are enjoyed for their taste, not because anyone must have them to survive the winter. Habit and pleasure, rather than necessity, have kept alive many of the foods that salt once made possible and that the old ways handed down.

In some inland and mountain regions, such as the Alps, the Himalayas and the Great Lakes area of North America, the soil and water contain very little iodine, and many people developed a swelling of the neck called goitre. It occurs because the thyroid gland needs iodine to make its hormones, and where the food supply lacks it, the gland grows larger in the attempt to cope. For centuries nobody understood why, and the condition was widely accepted as a part of life.

Between 1917 and 1922, the American doctor David Marine carried out a large trial among schoolgirls in Akron, Ohio, in which some children received small amounts of iodine and others did not. Goitre developed far less often among those who took it, and the result persuaded many health authorities that the problem could be prevented. The question that followed was how to give iodine to a whole population cheaply, and the answer turned out to be remarkably simple.

The answer was to add a very small amount of iodine to table salt, which almost everybody bought and used every day. Switzerland began to sell iodised salt in 1922, and the United States followed in 1924, and the scheme was soon copied by other countries. It was a simple and cheap solution to a problem that had troubled human beings for thousands of years, and it needed no new machines.

Iodised salt works so well because nearly everyone eats a little salt every day, in every region and at every level of income, so that the iodine reaches the whole population without any special effort. It costs very little and does not change the taste, and it protects not only the neck but also the brain, since a lack of iodine during pregnancy can harm a baby's development. Few public health measures in history have been so simple, so cheap or so successful as this one, and its success was largely unseen.

Today many countries encourage or require the use of iodised salt, and goitre has become rare in places where it was once very common. In some regions, however, people still do not get enough iodine, and international health workers continue to try to reach them. The humble salt shaker, once a symbol of power, has found a modern role as a quiet guardian of children's health, which few of its first users could have imagined.

Today, in a strange reversal, many people eat more salt than their bodies need, and a high intake is linked with high blood pressure, which can in turn raise the risk of heart disease and stroke. The World Health Organization suggests that adults take less than about five grams of salt a day, which is roughly a teaspoon, though most of the salt in many diets comes from packaged and restaurant food, not the shaker. This is general information only, and anyone who is worried about their own diet or blood pressure should ask a doctor.

Today the world produces hundreds of millions of tonnes of salt every year, an amount that would have astonished the caravan drivers of the Sahara and the boiling-house workers of Cheshire. It comes from vast solar ponds, from deep mines and from brine wells, and countries such as China, the United States and India are among the largest producers. The scale of the trade is far beyond anything that the ancient world could have imagined.

Surprisingly, only a small part of all the salt produced in the world is used in food. The bulk goes to chemical factories, which turn it into chlorine, caustic soda and a host of other substances, while the rest is used for treating water, for animal feed and for clearing the roads in winter. The shaker on the table is therefore the smallest customer of a very large industry.

In cold countries, trucks spread salt on the roads in winter, because salty water freezes at a lower temperature than fresh water, and a layer of ice can therefore melt even in the frost. It saves lives by making roads safer, but the salt that washes away enters rivers and soil, and it also eats into metal bridges and the bodies of cars. Engineers continue to search for gentler ways of keeping the roads open, and some cities now use salty water or sand for the purpose.

In the high Andes of Bolivia lies the Salar de Uyuni, the largest salt flat on Earth, a dazzling white plain that in the rainy season becomes a vast mirror reflecting the sky. Beneath its crust lies brine rich in lithium, a metal that is used in the batteries of phones, laptops and electric cars, and the mining of it raises questions about water, land and the interests of the local people. The old story of salt, which began with hunters following deer, has found a new and unexpected chapter in the age of the battery.

On the supermarket shelf, sea salt, rock salt, flaky salt and fine table salt may look quite different, and they are sold at very different prices, but they are all mostly sodium chloride. They differ mainly in the size of their crystals, in the trace of other minerals they contain and in the way they taste and feel on the tongue. The chef may care a great deal about those differences, but the chemist will point out that the substance underneath is essentially the same.

Salt lost its political power when it ceased to be scarce, which happened as railways, steamships and modern mines delivered it in huge quantities to every part of the world. A commodity that had once been precious enough to tax, guard and fight over could now be bought for the price of a few sweets, and no ruler could build an empire on the commerce in it. Cheapness, in the end, was the great victory of the people who needed it.

In many countries a kilogram of salt now costs only a few coins, which makes it one of the cheapest and most plentiful items in the shop. Nobody guards it with soldiers, nobody smuggles it across the border, and a family can buy a year's supply without noticing the expense. Yet the cheapness of salt is itself a human achievement, and it has taken thousands of years of labour to bring it about.

The memory of salt survives in our everyday speech, in words such as salary and salad and in phrases that we use without thinking about their history. We say that a reliable person is worth his salt or is the salt of the earth, we talk of rubbing salt into a wound, and we advise each other to take a doubtful story with a grain of salt. Such phrases are like fossils, and they preserve the memory of a time when salt mattered deeply to every household.

A single grain of salt on a plate may have begun its life in an ancient sea, lain buried under rock for millions of years and then been dug up or dried from the water of a living ocean. It passed through the hands of miners and pond workers, through factories and ships, across a shop counter and into a kitchen, and each stage depended on the skill and labour of people who never met. Behind every pinch lies a long chain of human work, and most of the people in it will never know that you tasted the result.

Salt marked out the roads of ancient Rome, enriched the kingdoms of Africa, filled the treasuries of emperors and kings, and in the end gave a movement for freedom its most memorable symbol. Its story reminds us that the greatest forces in history are often hidden in the most ordinary things, and that a humble commodity can carry great power. The next time you reach for the shaker at the table, you will be holding a little of that story in your hand.
